A Northerner can represent me with both justice and insight, and the fact that this now seems strange to some is itself proof of how thoroughly modern activists and organizations like the SPLC have seized control of our history. They have reduced a complex American life to a crude symbol of slavery, and their narrative has even swayed certain self-styled "Lost Causers" who insist I must stand only for disunion. My own record shows otherwise: I labored to preserve the Union until Mississippi required my services, and I answered that call because I believed a state possessed the constitutional right to withdraw.

No better evidence of fair Northern judgment exists than General Morris Schaff’s 1922 biography. A Union veteran who had fought under Grant produced the most balanced and humane study of me yet written. Contemporary reviewers, Northern and Southern alike, praised its sympathy, its refusal of caricature, and its clear-eyed assessment of both my strengths and limitations. Schaff’s work remains a standing rebuke to those who claim only one section can understand me.

Other Northern voices followed the same path. James Redpath, once a committed abolitionist, later offered measured and public praise that helped rehabilitate my reputation. Professor Edward Channing of Harvard, one of the leading historians of his generation, examined my motives and abilities without sectional prejudice and found them worthy of respect. Even the formal restoration of my citizenship was led by a senator from Oregon who called the earlier denial a grave injustice inflicted by a vindictive conqueror.

National honors tell the same story. President Ronald Reagan publicly endorsed the rededication of a monument to me in my native Kentucky. When my statue was placed in the United States Capitol, Northern newspapers welcomed it as proof that the old sectional bitterness had faded, and the dedication itself was framed as the final link binding the country together. These recognitions did not arise from Southern nostalgia alone; they required the assent and often the initiative of men and women north of the Potomac.

Ironically, some of the earliest and most bitter critics of my leadership were the very writers later labeled “Lost Cause” authors. Edward Pollard attacked me with sustained personal hostility and blamed me for the Confederacy’s defeat. The modern claim that my memory belongs exclusively to one narrow ideology is therefore a recent invention. 

Fair-minded Northerners long helped secure my place in the national story. That a Northerner should continue that work today is not anomalous—it is consistent with the historical record. The real anomaly is the recent capture of my image by those who prefer activist caricature to evidence.

text:
Portrait of a Gentleman By OneGeneral Schaff’s “Jefferson Davis” is Perhaps the Best Biography of Him Yet Written.

It is a matter worthy of comment that the most sympathetic and at the same time most unbiased study of the president of the Confederacy should come from the pen of a union soldier, one who went to the battlefields of Virginia direct from West Point at a most impressionable age. More than this, the book is easily the best study of Mr. Davis that has yet appeared. I know of no other that can be compared to it, viewed in the large. It probably comes nearer the final appraisal of history than any other, and it deserves a wide reading by both admirers and critics of Mr. Davis.'

Those who are familiar with “The Spirit of Old West Point,” “The Battle of the Wilderness,” and “The Sunset of the Confederacy,” by the same author need no introduction to him nor any testimonial of his fitness for the task. Devoted and loyal to the cause of the union as he has ever been, the south could ask no fairer interpreter. His readers have learned already to admire his qualities as an investigator and writer; they know, too, one special fitness which he possesses for this particular work. His opening paragraphs, besides indicating the spirit in which he approaches his subject, bear witness to this:

“There are two reasons for undertaking to write this book. The first and main one is this: A longing to see justice done, so far as my pen may prevail, to Jefferson Davis, president of the ill-starred Southern Confederacy, who, I feel and believe, has had unfair treatment by the historians of the great war between the states, known as the Southern Rebellion, and against whose armies I fought on many fields, including the bloody ones of Chancellorsville, the Wilderness and Spotsylvania. So then it is not through sympathy with the cause he was at the head of that I take up my pen; no, but at the entreaty of two mighty advocates, Truth and Fair Play. I am cheered on, furthermore, in my undertaking by one of the handsomest, the noblest of our country’s virtues, Magnanimity, proclaiming that out of hatred and revenge to perpetuate a false and unjust portrait of the leader of the Confederacy, whose sons and grandsons of whose gallant defenders helped so bravely to carry their united country’s flag to victory on the fields of France, is unworthy and out of keeping with a great-hearted people. Moreover, Jefferson Davis, besides being leader in the most unparalleled struggle of modern times—a struggle commemorated by monuments, ceremonial, and poetry that deck the green slopes of that height called history—was in manner and reality, in private and public life, the finest product of a democracy; namely, a gentleman. The world has had many types of the hero, statesman, and philosopher, but only one in its conception of the gentleman. Again, his mind was not only stored with political, scientific, and historic knowledge but ornamented also with the ripened fruits and beauties of literature; and his heart, the mind’s working companion, was naturally bold and had not only stood the dangers of the battlefield but was strong also with the finest chords of sweet tenderness. The second reason is the silent personal pleasure that will attend the use of my pen in such a cause, not arguing or contending, but talking as it were to an open-minded reader who, I hope, on taking up this book is blessed with a light heart; but should he be so unfortunate as to be harassed by cares and sorrows will, while reading it, forget them all and find his pillow sweet.”

The volume might well be called “The Biography of a Gentleman,” and surely no one is better qualified than General Schaff to write such a book. Just as it is necessary, in the words of an old adage, to “set a thief to catch a thief,” so, if we wish to have portrayed the life of a gentleman, we must find a gentleman to undertake the task. And no one could ever adequately interpret Jefferson Davis who was not himself a gentleman. So it is because General Schaff himself, as well as Jefferson Davis, is so completely described in the quotation that he has been able to prepare so unique and altogether worthy a study of a splendid, though much-maligned, figure of American history.

The story of Mr. Davis’s life prior to his election as president of the Confederacy occupies substantially half the book. Here are given in sufficient detail the events of these years. But the striking value of this part of the story lies in its picture of the making of the man, its tracing of the forces which shaped him, the influences which entered into his public career and private life, and the very making of his convictions. 

Take as an illustration the explanation of a characteristic of Mr. Davis which was of infinite importance in his later life, which influenced the very history of the Confederacy. Describing the spirit of West Point and showing its tendency to make its graduates aristocratic and exclusive, to cut them off from the great body of the people, he says:

“Now such was the inborn nature of Jefferson Davis that while all the virtues of West Point education, honor, frankness, truthfulness, and good manners found a native soil to grow in, still in it too were already germinated seeds of a certain reserve and dignity that found the air congenial and flourished by the time he graduated into a distinctive aristocratic bearing that clung to him to the end; and much, very much, as all the world knows to his serious disadvantage in his presidential life.”

Many mis-statements as to Davis are here corrected, but, except for those of fundamental importance, these need not be discussed here. That he was a fire-eater, the leader of the group in the south which was resolved to bring about sectional separation, and even war, at any cost. Well-informed people know better, but most people—and this is true of the south as well as the north—are not well-informed about Jefferson Davis. The author shows conclusively how bent he was on peace and union, at the sacrifice of everything save the fundamental safety of his section, as he construed it, and honor.

The picture of the difficulties which Mr. Davis had to face—those which he solved and those which, under all the circumstances, were beyond solution—is excellently drawn. That he was severe with Johnston, Beauregard, and Bragg goes without saying. I may add that, in my opinion, the book does not suffer in value therefrom.

Probably the most striking chapter of the volume is the one dealing with the charge that Davis was, to use the words of Blaine, “knowingly, deliberately, and willfully of the gigantic murder and crime of Andersonville.” The author shows that Davis, no less than Lee, was steadfast in his purpose not to tolerate any policy of retaliation for outrages, that even in the case of the prisoners taken in the Dahlgren raid which had for its purpose the burning of Richmond and the assassination of Davis and his cabinet, he insisted upon their immunity from punishment because they were prisoners of war. He shows too that Davis, in spite of his austerity of manner, was essentially as tender-hearted as Lincoln himself. Finally, he shows that Davis sought in every way to maintain a system of exchanging prisoners and that it was defeated by General Grant’s orders which were sustained by President Lincoln.

“It is a matter of fact, Confederate authorities throughout that autumn (1864) when the captives were falling like the leaves of a white ash the morning after a frost, plead and plead for exchange, offering at last to let every one go home without equivalent. The south can without fear or hesitation appeal to the official war records as to the desire and will of the Confederate war department to mitigate the horrible conditions.“

Authors of repute have seen fit to incorporate in their histories of the war, moving accounts of the suffering in the southern camps and the ghastly spectacle of their victims; accompanied, furthermore, by extracts from letters, written by prominent persons to Davis, protesting conditions in some camps as a shame and dishonor; thereby, with infernal malice, thrusting him into the picture with all its speaking condemnation. But they have not described the like sufferings of the ghastly spectacle of hollow-eyed prisoners in northern camps, or delivery; nor have they given extracts from letters written by clergymen and men of prominence to Mr. Lincoln, censuring him for refusal to exchange, all of which can be found in the same volume of official war records.

“If, as has been said before, Mr. Davis is to be held responsible for the dead northern prisoners merely because he was commander-in-chief of the Confederate armies, may not Mr. Lincoln by similar reasoning be held responsible for the southern dead in northern prison camps?”

In still another way the book has a striking value. It depends on the best of grounds Mr. Davis’s position in respect to the peace proposals of 1864, and shows, what many students of the period have long ago concluded, that in spite of the prolongation of suffering and the increased mortality it was better for the whole thing to be fought out to a final conclusion.

It has been the fashion in the north and to some extent in the south to censure Davis for his course after the war. General Schaff describes in a telling way the imprisonment of Davis, the failure to try him and his release on bail, and the later events of his life. So far from accepting the view above referred to, he thus concludes his description of those years during which an arch of good-will came to span north and south:

“Next to Grant I believe that Davis by the friendliness of his bearing and candor in intercourse with northern men of influence and character, by urging his people on all occasions to obey the laws, and above all by refraining in addressing associations of veterans from saying anything to re-kindle the fagots of animosities, contributed more than any one man to the accomplishment of that great national achievement.”

It is a fine and human picture that he draws here, a superb portrait of an essentially great man. It is more. Discriminating readers will find in it—and rejoice to find—a splendid portrait of the gallant soldier and gentleman who wrote the book.
-J. G. de R.
-from the Greensboro Daily News (NC, 11/12/1922)

It is wild how quickly the news cycle moves. Not too long ago, everyone was hyper-focused on  .@SenMcConnell’s absence, but now that conversation has completely faded from the spotlight. 

The initial shock has worn off, the noise has quieted down, and Kentucky is staring down a massive reality check. 

In exactly sixty-eight days, we go to the polls, and the stakes could not be higher. 

This vote isn’t just about the broader direction of the country, it’s about a defining moment for our state as we choose who will fill McConnell’s seat in the Senate.

For Kentuckians, the choice ahead is a massive fork in the road because the two men running couldn't be further apart.

On one side, you have .@RepAndyBarr , who represents a predictable, deeply traditional conservative path. 

His platform relies on familiar Republican principles like cutting regulations, keeping taxes low, and backing traditional industries that have kept Kentucky's economy anchored for decades. 

Voting for Barr is a vote for stability, a predictable business-friendly environment, and a firm continuation of conservative control.

On the other side is  .@Booker4KY, who offers a total rejection of the status quo. 

Booker brings a progressive vision that explicitly aligns with .@DemSocialist, He is pushing for massive structural changes, from universal healthcare and heavy investments in green energy to aggressive social safety nets funded by restructuring how wealth is distributed. 

He isn't looking to tweak the current system—he wants to rebuild it from the ground up to focus heavily on working-class communities.

This isn't a race where you can just sit on the fence or vote on autopilot. 

It is a fundamental debate about what Kentucky should look like for the next generation. 

You are either choosing to double down on the established conservative economic model with Barr, or you are choosing a radical leap toward a progressive, government-backed safety net with Booker. 

It is going to be a fascinating sixty-eight days, and the future of the Commonwealth is entirely in our hands.

CHETTER DISPATCH – EDITION 0287
July 30, 2026
THE FAMILY THAT FOUND THE CASH REGISTER

So, let me see if I've got this straight.

The government is always "broke" when we need something.

Healthcare? Too expensive.

Housing? Good luck.

But when the powerful need a government contract, a sweetheart deal, or a $400 million airplane from a foreign government?

Suddenly, Washington finds its checkbook.

Funny how that works.

And then there's the Trump family.

The Trumps have spent generations learning something most of us never got the opportunity to study:

How to turn proximity to government into money.

Fred Trump built his real estate empire with substantial help from government-backed housing programs.

Donald Trump took that family playbook and turned it into a global brand.

Now his children are investing in defense companies doing billions of dollars in business with the federal government.

And Donald Trump is sitting in the Oval Office.

What could possibly go wrong?

Well, how about the appearance that the people closest to power keep finding themselves remarkably close to the money?

Let's talk numbers.

Forbes estimates Donald Trump's net worth at roughly $6.4 billion as of late July 2026. Forbes also reported that he generated approximately $2.4 billion in income and asset-sale proceeds in 2025 alone.

That's billion.

With a B.

Meanwhile, plenty of Americans are trying to stretch a paycheck until the end of the month without it snapping in half.

But hey, at least somebody's doing well.

Then there are the Trump sons.

A Washington Post investigation found that investment funds linked to Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump have invested in more than a dozen defense technology companies.

Those companies have generated at least $3.2 billion in direct government business since the investments were made, with another $3.1 billion in future contract options.

To be fair, the companies say they won the contracts on merit. Some contracts also existed before the Trump sons invested.

Fair enough.

But if your family is financially connected to companies seeking billions in government contracts while your father is president, people are going to have questions.

That's not partisan.

That's common sense.

Then came the jet.

Qatar offered the United States a Boeing 747 reportedly worth around $400 million for potential use as Air Force One.

The Pentagon accepted it.

Now it needs extensive security and communications modifications that could cost hundreds of millions more.

Meanwhile, the Trump family's business interests have expanded into Qatar.

Again, perhaps everything is perfectly legal.

But when did "it's legal" become the gold standard for ethical behavior?

I don't want my government operating by the philosophy of:

Well, technically, nobody went to jail.

That's a pretty low bar for the greatest democracy on Earth.

And this isn't just about Donald Trump.

It's about a system that has become far too comfortable with money influencing power, regardless of which party is in charge.

The family gets richer.

The powerful get access.

The contracts keep coming.

The deals keep multiplying.

And we're told to trust the process.

Meanwhile, the rest of us are standing in the grocery store doing mental gymnastics over a carton of eggs.

We're told healthcare is too expensive.

Housing is too expensive.

Government programs are too expensive.

But somehow, when the people at the top want something, the money appears.

Funny.

It's almost like Washington has two checkbooks.

One for the American people.

And one for everyone else.

Guess which one seems to have the bigger balance?

Government belongs to the people.

Not billionaires.

Not corporations.

Not political parties.

Not foreign governments.

And certainly not any family sitting close enough to the cash register to hear it ring.

We are the taxpayers.

We fund the government.

We pay the bills.

We are the employers.

And if an employee's family keeps getting richer while that employee is in charge of handing out the company's money, you can bet the shareholders are going to start asking questions.

A lot of questions.

That's not politics.

That's accountability.

So here's mine:

Who is government really working for?

Because if it isn't working for the American people, then we have a much bigger problem than the Trump family.

We have a government that has forgotten who the boss is.

And perhaps it's time we reminded them.

Until next time,
Chetter
@ChetterHub

One voice. One dispatch. One message:

Government belongs to the people. Not to the powerful. Not to the wealthy. And not to any family that mistakes public service for a private business opportunity.

It’s honestly insane that I feel the need to post this, but an LSU fan doxxed me last year to a small group of people and it has spread outward since.. so I’d love to address all of the “state fan” allegations, especially since my account has grown so much over the past year or so. 

Everyone has a story. I’d like to share mine since the LSU fans on here (and some Ole Miss fans) have been in my mentions and quotes about this ever since 2025. 

I am a Mississippi native. My parents did not go to college, so I did not grow up ingrained in a family of Ms State or Ole Miss fans.. I got to choose who I wanted to root for. 

I grew up an hour from Tuscaloosa, an hour 20 from Starkville, and 3 hours away from Oxford. I began playing peewee football at a young age and then began to watch college football and the NFL, as one does. I was hooked on football but didn’t have a team to root for. 

My aunt lives in New Albany Mississippi and her son, my first cousin (who is quite a bit older than me) went to Ole Miss. When we would visit in the fall we would go to Ole Miss football games. My first experience of an Ole Miss football game was Jacksonville State in 2010. What a welcome to college football. I attended the BYU game the next year. I started 0-2 as a rebel fan 😂

As soon as I stepped on campus for that first game, I fell in love with Ole Miss. the hospitality, the grove, the band, it all hit me like a ton of bricks. The game was terrible as we all know, but I became a fan from that day forward. I rooted for Ole Miss from then on. 

I was set to graduate high school in 2017. My parents did not have money to send me to college so me and my twin brother were on our own in that category. I applied to Ole Miss, State, and several other schools and explored their scholarship opportunities. I was so excited to get the admission letter from ole miss; however I was going to have to pay for my school with student loans if I chose to go to Oxford. 

The community college in my town offered free tuition to all county school graduates. I thought that was a no brainer. From there, there was a state branch in my town that offered free tuition to the community college graduates. I also took this opportunity and graduated from the Mississippi State branch with a free bachelors degree in business administration .. all while going to Oxford on the weekends to cheer for the Rebs. 

I say all this to say, just because I did not attend Ole Miss does not mean I am any less of a fan than anyone who attended the university from their freshman to senior year. Everyone has a unique life path. I could have chosen to root for any school I wanted, but I chose at a young age to be a rebel fan. I have attended countless games including some of our biggest wins and worst losses and spent hundreds of weekends and thousands of dollars in Oxford and plan to continue until I die. I spend the money now that I could have spent paying back student loans giving to @grovecollectnil 😂

I am as much of an Ole Miss rebel as anyone in the fan base.. I just didn’t go into debt to do it. If you think that makes me less of a fan, so be it.. I truly do not care. I’ll still be in VHS and in road stadiums every Saturday that I can be cheering on MY Rebs.

This is not an official story and it never happened. I was never there.

Officials at the U.S. Army Medical Research Institute of Infectious Diseases (USAMRIID) received several non-human bodies recovered from a crash site in South Vietnam in 1968. These bodies resembled popular descriptions of "Grays." They were quietly transferred to the Institute for comparative anatomy for autopsy.

The wreckage, according to a heavily redacted after-action report included in the leaked documents was described as a "glowing disk that smelled like hot pennies and fish sauce."  It was discovered by a patrol that originally thought they had found a downed Soviet helicopter that, according to one soldier quoted in the report looked like it "had been redesigned by someone who hated aerodynamics."

The recovered remains were packed in ice, flown out under a cover story involving "unusual livestock," and delivered to USAMRIID because, a source close to the investigation said, "Fort Detrick already had the freezers and people who don’t ask questions." 

Preliminary findings, described in a leaked memo titled "Notes on Specimen V-68-A through D."

The "eyes" are not eyes. What look like large, dark ocular structures are, in fact, paired tympanic organs. Researchers concluded this after a technician sneezed and neural activity was detected in the specimen. Repeated experiments confirmed this. "They don’t see with those," the memo states. "They hear with their faces." This explains the complete lack of pupils and also why the crash may have been caused by a nearby artillery barrage that, to them, may have sounded like "God dropping a piano."

The blood is an overachiever. The oxygen-carrying molecule is a hybrid pigment containing both iron (hemoglobin-like) and copper (hemocyanin-like) centers. Samples were described as "a color that should not exist in nature and does not photograph well." Under different lighting the fluid shifted from rust-brown to blue-green. One lab tech allegedly muttered, "It’s like the animal couldn’t decide if it wanted to be a person or a horseshoe crab, so it did both and then joined the war."

The heart has three chambers. A single ventricle and two atria -- A classic amphibian layout, except scaled up and attached to vessels that "looked expensive."  Circulation is probably inefficient by human standards.

No photographs were included in the leak. A spokesperson from the Institute "neither confirms nor denies the existence of extra-terrestrial amphibians with facial ears and indecisive blood." All further questions were directed to a the public relations office. Repeated call to the number were answered by a vending machine in Building 1425.

Veterans of the original recovery team, reached for comment through a VFW hall that requested anonymity, offered only this: "We thought it was a new kind of mine. Then it flinched at the sound of a radio and we figure we had something" 

The Pentagon’s official position remains that no unidentified craft crashed in Vietnam, no bodies were shipped to Maryland, and if they were, they were almost certainly a species of large gecko with excellent echo-location.

Trump unveils new Air Force One, a converted Qatari 747
This article is more than 2 months old
New craft, called VC-25B Bridge, had provoked protest since $400m jet wildly exceeds limit on unsolicited gifts

Edward Helmore
Sat 20 Jun 2026 00.05 BST

Donald Trump unveiled the new, temporary Air Force One at a hangar at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Friday, a day after White House officials said farewell to one of two Boeing 747s used to transport presidents for more than 30 years.

The new jet, designated VC-25B and decked out in a punchy red, white, dark blue and gold livery, was gifted to Trump by the Gulf emirate of Qatar, provoking howls of political protest since the $400m jet wildly exceeds the limit on unsolicited gifts of $50 in value in a single calendar year from the same source.

Trump dismissed criticism of the arrangement, saying it would be “stupid” to turn down the offer. Then Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had said that “the secretary of defense has accepted a Boeing 747 from Qatar in accordance with all federal rules and regulations”.

The cost of converting the Qatari 747 has been put at $1bn, and it is designed to serve as a “bridge” aircraft until two long-delayed presidential Boeings are delivered in 2027 and 2028. The cost of the two purpose-built aircraft have ballooned from $3.7bn to $5bn.

Criticism of the gifted Qatari jet, which the Gulf state had previously tried to sell without success, included accusations that the costs of conversion could divert money from Sentinel, an ICBM (intercontinental ballistic missile) modernization program already running years behind schedule.

At the unveiling, Trump thanked the emir of Qatar. “He’s a fantastic guy,” he said. “He went through a lot over the last few months.”

“This is considered ​the world’s most luxurious plane,” Trump added. “When it was built, it was built at a level that will probably never be seen again.”

Trump has argued that the new jet was necessary to keep pace with more modern aircraft flown by foreign leaders. “These countries have a lot of respect for us, and yet they have a plane that’s much newer ​and much better. It’s a little ridiculous,” Trump said.

The two ageing 747s in the presidential fleet entered service in 1990, during the presidency of George HW Bush.

Earlier this year, one of the pair was forced to turn back to Washington on a trip to Davos, Switzerland, owing to a technical fault. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt told reporters that the crew identified a “minor electrical issue” and chose to turn around and return to the Andrews base.

The air force fast-tracked the retrofitting of the Qatari jet, but has skipped some planned modifications for the next-generation presidential jet in order to deliver an interim version sooner. Officials said it was up to presidential standards.

“The safety and security of the commander in chief is our highest priority,” Troy Meink, secretary of the air force, said in a statement on Friday. “From the beginning, we meticulously evaluated every requirement to accelerate delivery while maintaining the high standards expected of the presidential mission.“

The new jet, with a color-scheme that echoes that of Trump’s own jet, arrives two weeks before a planned formation flight over Washington DC on 4 July to celebrate the nation’s 250th anniversary. Trump told the crowd at Andrews that the new aircraft will lead the “biggest flyover in American history”.

A tour of the interior given to reporters on Friday revealed that its decor includes a framed print of a duck swimming in the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool.

The delivery of the Qatari jet crosses over with the retirement of the Air Force One tail number 29000, the Boeing 747-200 that transported the president back from Europe on Thursday and is ultimately destined for a museum.

#Space #Cosmos
 NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is set to launch this weekend. When will we see its first photos?  https://t.co/6rtu53HNkd 

NASA's next-generation cosmic observatory — the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope — is set to launch this weekend on a potentially decade-long mission to hunt for distant exoplanets, map out the Milky Way and unravel some of the universe's biggest mysteries, such as the true nature of dark matter. 

The Roman telescope and its payload are scheduled to lift off aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket Sunday (Aug. 30) at 7:26 a.m. EDT from Launch Complex 39A at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, according to NASA. A few hours later, the telescope will be released from the rocket's second stage and be exposed to the vacuum of space for the first time. 

But even if everything goes according to plan, we will still have to wait a while to get a glimpse of Roman's first groundbreaking images.

As of Thursday morning (Aug. 27), the National Weather Service forecasts a 50% chance of thunderstorms at Kennedy Space Center Sunday, so weather could delay the launch. If that happens, a second launch window is available Monday (Aug. 31) at 7:22 a.m. EDT, when there is a reduced risk of thunderstorms.

You can watch the event on a SpaceX livestream and stay up to date with last-minute developments and postlaunch news via a live blog from Live Science's sister site https://t.co/henl6sE9wi.

Roman stands 42 feet tall and weighs around the same as a fully grown T. rex. This photo was taken on Dec. 4, 2025, shortly after the spacecraft was fully constructed. (Image credit: NASA/Jolearra Tshiteya)

What is the Roman Space Telescope?

The Roman Space Telescope is NASA's latest flagship observatory. It follows the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), which launched in 2021, and the Hubble Space Telescope, which has been in orbit since 1990. Rather than replacing those spacecraft, Roman will work alongside them to help scientists scour the skies like never before.

The observatory is named after pioneering scientist Nancy Grace Roman, who served as NASA's first chief astronomer between 1960 and 1979. It is approximately 42 feet (12.7 meters) tall and 14 feet (4.4 m) wide and weighs around 18,000 pounds (8,000 kilograms) — about the same as a fully grown Tyrannosaurus rex, according to a NASA fact sheet.

Roman was fully completed in December 2025, almost a decade after construction began and within its initial $4.3 billion budget (less than half what JWST cost). Since then, it has been moved more than 900 miles (1,450 kilometers) from Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland and undergone a series of final checks in NASA's "clean rooms." Having initially been slated for a 2027 liftoff, the telescope is technically launching ahead of schedule.

Roman was encased in its protective fairing earlier this week, ahead of its proposed launch on Sunday (Aug. 30). (Image credit: NASA/Sydney Rohde (Rocz))

Roman will eventually be stationed around 1 million miles (1.6 million km) from Earth at what scientists call a Lagrange point — a fixed point relative to our planet where the gravity of two objects cancels out. Its specific Lagrange point will be Sun-Earth L2, where JWST and the European Space Agency's Gaia and Euclid space telescopes already reside.

Roman's initial mission will last five years, but experts hope it could survive at least twice that long. Some space telescopes far outlast their initial missions; for example, Hubble is more than two decades past its original mission parameters, and NASA's recently doomed Swift Observatory lasted 10 times longer than predicted. 

What makes Roman special?

Roman has two key instruments that set it apart from its predecessors. The first is its Wide Field Instrument, a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 meters) mirror, which gives it a field of view 100,000 times greater than Hubble's. It will also see the cosmos in infrared light, similar to JWST. These combined capabilities will allow Roman to observe the cosmos like never before.

But the telescope's secret weapon is arguably its coronagraph, which can block out the light from distant stars, allowing Roman to see fainter objects, such as the exoplanets that orbit these stars. Until now, scientists' main way of finding alien worlds was to wait for them to pass in front of, or transit, their home star, but Roman will be able to directly image exoplanets at almost any time in their orbital cycles. (Exoplanets remain out of view when they are directly behind their home stars.)

Roman's Wide Field Instrument utilizes a 7.9-foot-wide mirror to focus infrared light into a 288-megapixel camera that has a field of view 100,000 times greater than Hubble's. (Image credit: NASA/Chris Gunn)

One of the biggest and most exciting claims researchers have made about Roman is that it could help reveal up to 100,000 exoplanets. Such discoveries would revolutionize how we study alien worlds, especially considering that we have uncovered over 6,000 exoplanets since the first one was spotted in 1992. 

However, the telescope will also conduct long-term surveys that will help astronomers accurately map the Milky Way and find extremely distant galaxies, potentially helping scientists solve the mysteries of dark matter and dark energy that currently underpin a "cosmological crisis" surrounding the universe's expansion. And as with any new space telescope, scientists will likely find novel ways of using Roman once it is in operation.

Roman will launch aboard one of SpaceX's Falcon Heavy rockets, which has a 100% success rate across its 12 launches to date.  (Image credit: SpaceX)

"The mission will offer practically limitless opportunities for astronomers to conduct a broad range of additional science," NASA representatives wrote in the fact sheet. "From objects in our outer solar system and exploding stars to growing black holes and galaxies by the billions, very little will be beyond Roman's reach."

The spacecraft will beam roughly 1.4 terabytes of data — roughly 10 times the storage capacity of an average smartphone — to ground stations across Earth every day, according to the fact sheet. 

When will we see Roman's first photos?

Roman's first snaps are arguably the most anticipated astronomical images since the debut photos from the ground-based Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which were released in June 2025. 

Roman will launch from Launch Complex TK on Sunday (Aug. 30). This photo shows one of these rockets, equipped with NASA's Europa Clipper probe, lifting off from Florida's Kennedy Space Center on Oct. 14, 2024. (Image credit: CHANDAN KHANNA/AFP via Getty Images)

But first, Roman has to travel to its Lagrange point, which is roughly four times farther away than the moon. This could take several weeks, although no exact timeline has been provided.   

RELATED STORIES

Once Roman is in position, there will be a roughly 90-day commissioning period, during which the telescope will fully power up its instruments and run a series of diagnostic tests to ensure everything is in order before its mission truly begins. 

There is, therefore, a slim chance that we could see Rubin's first photos before the end of the year. However, NASA officials have tentatively predicted that the telescope will start snapping the stars in early 2027. It took JWST about seven months postlaunch to send its first full-color image to Earth.

NASA representatives have promised that "data from all of Roman's surveys will be made public as soon as it is processed, with no periods of exclusive access," so once the images are ready, everyone will be able to see them.

Reparations is not a plan.
It is a campaign ad.

The Left does not need a workable check. They need a promise big enough to keep Black voters in line and vague enough that they never have to cash it.
Gavin Newsom is the exhibit.

In 2020, after George Floyd, he signed the bill that created California’s first-in-the-nation reparations task force. That was the sale. California would “study” slavery’s legacy and “make amends.” The Black Caucus heard cash. Activists heard $1.2 million a head. Economists floated figures so large they would have blown a hole in a state already drowning in debt.
Newsom needed that energy. He was staring at a recall. He did not stand up and say, “I will write every Black Californian a seven-figure check.” He did the smarter thing. He lit the task force, talked structural racism, posed with the caucus, and let the rumor do the turnout work.

He survived the recall.
Then the bill came due.
The task force dumped a 1,000-page report. Direct payments. Racial-impact reviews of every law. A new racial bureaucracy. Newsom’s answer in 2023: “Dealing with the legacy of slavery is about much more than cash payments.”
Translation: the commercial already ran. Do not expect the product.

What he delivered instead was the politician’s special. A formal apology. A plaque. A Bureau for Descendants of American Slavery to verify ancestry. $6 million for CSU to study how to check family trees. Vetoes on college preferences, eminent-domain payouts, and a slice of a home-loan program, citing cost and “legal risks.”

That is the model.
Wave the word reparations when you need the vote.
Build a commission when you need a headline.
Veto the check when the budget and the Supreme Court show up.
It is the same play in Evanston, San Francisco, Maryland, and every presidential primary where a Democrat discovers slavery again for 48 hours. HR 40 has been introduced since 1989. Nobody passes the transfer. They pass the speech.

Black voters are not a ATM for 1860. They are citizens who need safe streets, working schools, and a job market that is not a racial spoils system. The Left offers a ghost IOU instead, because a ghost IOU does not require them to fix Oakland schools or stop releasing criminals.
Newsom got the recall behind him.

California still does not have the checks.
That was never the point.

I don’t think I’ve ever seen this before.

A doctor standing at a teenage cancer patient’s bedside, bowing his head, and praying over him before he leaves the hospital.

Many of you have been following 15-year-old Will Roberts’ courageous battle with Stage 4 osteosarcoma.

Will’s mom, Brittney, shared a moment she says her family will never forget.

She says Dr. James Flint has been part of Will’s journey since shortly after his diagnosis in January 2025.

At the time, Will’s family was in Alabama.

Dr. Flint was in California.

Even then, Brittney says he offered to answer questions, listen, and help however he could.

Months later, after God opened the door for Will to come to California for the experimental DeltaRex-G treatment, Dr. Flint became one of the physicians helping care for him at Rady Children’s Hospital in California.

Before Will left the hospital today, Dr. Flint gathered around his bedside with the family and prayed.

Not a quick prayer.

A heartfelt prayer over every part of Will’s fight.

He prayed for Will’s pain to be relieved.

He prayed for the fluid in his body to improve.

He prayed that healing would continue, that Will’s mobility would return, and that one day he’d be back outside in the sunshine… even out on a boat fishing again.

He prayed for wisdom for every doctor and nurse caring for Will.

He prayed for peace for Brittney and Jason as they continue walking beside their son.

And perhaps my favorite line of all…

“Lord, only You know the outcome.”

Brittney says this doctor has been part of one miracle after another in Will’s journey, helping open doors they never imagined possible.

“The whole story is nothing but God,” she wrote.

“These are the doctors that God led into our lives and will be a part of our story always.”

No matter your beliefs, it’s hard not to be moved by a physician who cares enough to stop, take his patient’s hand, and pray not only for healing, but for the simple things a 15-year-old boy dreams of doing again.

Please continue praying for Will.

Pray that the bleeding stops, the swelling improves, his body continues to heal, and that one day Dr. Flint’s prayer about seeing Will back in the sunshine with a fishing pole becomes reality

Austin Collie. Cody Hoffman. Ross Apo. McKay Jacobson.
​
Those are among the BYU receivers who cleared 400 receiving yards as freshmen. It is a short list for a reason — at BYU it almost never happens.
​
Which makes the question in front of this coaching staff a live one.
​
BYU returns Bear Bachmeier and LJ Martin, and brings back more defensive production than nearly any team in the country. Wide receiver is the one room where proven production did not come back.
​
So there is a real chance the Cougars lean on a freshman this fall. Jaron Pula or Legend Glasker.
​
BYU On SI went and checked whether that actually works anywhere.
​
In 2025, fifteen freshman wide receivers across the Power Four put up 400 or more receiving yards. Miami's Malachi Toney led them all with north of 1,200.
​
And they were not padding stats on bad teams. Miami. Oregon. Texas. USC. Alabama.
​
You can reach the College Football Playoff with freshmen in the receiver rotation. That is settled.
​
But the study found a catch worth sitting with.
​
Eight of the top ten were four-star recruits. If a freshman produces immediately, he was almost always a coveted recruit first.
​
Pula fits that profile precisely. Four-star, offers from around the country — and he left high school rated higher than Toney, the freshman who just led the nation.
​
He is already 200 pounds. What remains is the playbook and the trust of receivers coach Fesi Sitake.
​
Glasker is the harder bet on paper. He is a three-star.
​
Washington's Dezmen Roebuck and Wake Forest's Chris Barnes proved a three-star can do it. But there were dozens of three-star receivers in that class, and only a couple broke through.
​
And yet out of spring camp, Glasker was the freshman who looked most likely to break out.
​
History says the best BYU receivers find the field early. Neil Pau'u. Dax Milne. Gunner Romney. All contributed as freshmen.
​
Clearing 400 yards in year one is the rare part.
​
The conclusion is the useful part: BYU can chase a Big 12 championship with freshmen in the rotation, because the programs that do it recruit players ready on arrival.
​
BYU signed its best class of the modern era in December.
​
Fall camp opens shortly. Watch that room.
​
Credit where it belongs — the study is Casey Lundquist's at BYU On SI. Worth reading in full.
​

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

August 27, 2026

REPUBLICAN DETRANSITIONER ATTORNEY TO FILE FEDERAL CIVIL RIGHTS SUIT

AGAINST AMY P. CAMPANELLI, MUSKEGON COUNTY, AND THE STATE OF MICHIGAN

Michigan criminal defense attorney alleges the county rescinded an accepted public-defender position because of her protected political speech and gender-critical views

DETROIT, MICHIGAN - Michigan criminal defense attorney Hendrix Moise announced that she intends to file a federal civil rights lawsuit against Amy P. Campanelli, individually and in her official capacity as Public Defender Director of Muskegon County; the County of Muskegon; and the State of Michigan, after the county abruptly rescinded an Assistant Public Defender position Moise had already accepted.

Moise, a female detransitioner, Republican, and outspoken critic of gender ideology, alleges that the rescission was unconstitutional retaliation for her protected speech, political expression, and publicly stated gender-critical beliefs.

The employment offer was rescinded on August 21, 2026, by Amy P. Campanelli, just ten days after Moise accepted the position. The file had already been sent to Human Resources and an October 5, 2026 start date had been locked in.

THE HIRING AND THE RESCISSION

Moise interviewed for the Assistant Public Defender position twice in August 2026. Muskegon County extended a formal offer, which Moise accepted on August 11.

She then began restructuring her professional and personal life around the new job, including preparing to relocate to West Michigan, pursuing housing near Muskegon, altering her existing criminal-defense caseload and private practice, and taking other significant steps in reliance upon the county’s offer.

On August 21, Campanelli notified Moise that the offer was rescinded effective immediately. No substantive reason for the decision was provided.

Moise’s forthcoming lawsuit will seek to determine through discovery why the county reversed course, who participated in the rescission decision, what information concerning Moise was reviewed, and whether her political views, social-media speech, detransition advocacy, or gender-critical beliefs played a role.

“The government does not get to condition public employment on ideological conformity,” Moise said. “I am a female detransitioner. I am gender critical. I am a Republican. None of those things disqualifies me from being an excellent criminal defense attorney.”

THE CLAIMS

The anticipated complaint will assert claims under the First Amendment and 42 U.S.C. § 1983 against Campanelli and Muskegon County, as well as a claim of sex discrimination under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. State-law contract and promissory-estoppel claims arising from the accepted written offer will also be pleaded. The State of Michigan is named for prospective injunctive relief.

The Supreme Court has already held that an assistant public defender may not be hired or fired for political belief. Branti v. Finkel, 445 U.S. 507 (1980); Rutan v. Republican Party of Illinois, 497 U.S. 62 (1990). The Sixth Circuit has held that the debate over sex, gender identity, and pronouns is a matter of public concern. Meriwether v. Hartop, 992 F.3d 492 (6th Cir. 2021).

WHO CAMPANELLI IS - THE COOK COUNTY RECORD

Campanelli is not a career-long Muskegon official. She was the Public Defender of Cook County, Illinois, from 2015 until spring 2021, when Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle declined to reappoint her. Contemporary reporting described the exit as a forced departure after she sought but did not win a second term.

In July 2023, the Cook County Inspector General’s Office, then led by interim Inspector General Steven E. Cyranoski, released a summary finding that Campanelli “misused confidential information” by routinely releasing identifying details of children defended by her office. According to reporting by Injustice Watch and the Chicago Sun-Times, those disclosures included names, dates of birth, contact information, and pending charges of juvenile clients.

The Inspector General found that Campanelli signed a December 3, 2020 information-sharing agreement with the Lawndale Christian Legal Center - without the court authorization required under the Illinois Juvenile Court Act - to help enroll as many as 40 public-defender clients a month in a study tied to the nonprofit’s grant funding. Campanelli sat on the organization’s advisory board while still Cook County Public Defender. Weeks after she left office, she became the nonprofit’s Vice President of Restorative Justice. The Inspector General reported that the disclosures also violated Cook County personnel rules and its ethics ordinance, and noted that a willful violation of the Juvenile Court Act is a Class C misdemeanor, with each violation subject to a $1,000 fine. Campanelli declined to cooperate with the Inspector General’s investigators. Her attorney later said the office’s policy was to obtain informed consent from juvenile clients and their parents.

The Inspector General recommended referral to the Illinois Attorney Registration and Disciplinary Commission. The ARDC investigated Campanelli and Lawndale executive director Cliff Nellis and, in December 2023, sent close-out letters stating the investigation was complete and that no disciplinary action would be taken at that time. No court has convicted Campanelli of a crime arising from the Inspector General’s findings.

Campanelli was also a named defendant, in her official capacity as Cook County Public Defender, in Brown v. Cook County, a federal class action brought by female assistant public defenders who alleged that county officials failed to protect them from repeated sexual misconduct by male detainees at the Cook County Jail - including masturbation, indecent exposure, grabbing, and the emission of bodily fluids. Cook County approved an approximately $14 million settlement of that suit in 2020. Campanelli later told Injustice Watch she believed she had done everything in her power, that the jail was the sheriff’s responsibility, and that she was “very unfairly treated” by being named in the lawsuit.

In February 2020, a nearly 28-year veteran of Campanelli’s office, Assistant Public Defender Ingrid Gill-Richards, sued Campanelli individually and in her official capacity, along with other supervisors and Cook County, in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois. Gill-Richards v. Campanelli, No. 20 C 00822 (N.D. Ill.) (Tharp, J.). Gill-Richards alleged that after she reported sexual harassment by a division chief and filed charges with the Cook County Equal Employment Opportunity Office, the Illinois Department of Human Rights, and the EEOC, Campanelli scoured her emails and documents looking for a reason to fire her, subjected her work to extra review, reported her to the Illinois Attorney Registration and Disciplinary Commission, and terminated her on February 4, 2019. Gill-Richards also alleged she was targeted after she disclosed a conflict and potential ineffective-assistance issues in a post-conviction matter involving other assistant public defenders in the office. In a January 2022 written opinion, Judge John J. Tharp, Jr., denied in part the defendants’ motion to dismiss and allowed Title VII retaliation claims against Cook County, among other claims, to proceed. Those are allegations in a filed federal complaint; no verdict establishing liability is cited here.

Muskegon County appointed Campanelli Public Defender Director effective June 10, 2024.

“The official who just used government hiring power to punish a woman for saying sex is real is the same official Cook County’s own Inspector General found misused confidential information about children her office was sworn to defend,” Moise said. “She was a named defendant in a $14 million case about female public defenders being sexually abused on the job. A nearly 30-year female assistant public defender sued her for allegedly hunting through that lawyer’s emails after the lawyer reported sexual harassment - and then firing her. She does not get to lecture me about fitness to represent poor people.”

WHY THE SPEECH IS PROTECTED

Moise identified and lived as a transgender man for approximately seven years before detransitioning. She now speaks publicly about that experience and has become an outspoken critic of gender ideology and of the informed-consent medicalization model.

“Detransitioners are often encouraged to tell our stories only so long as those stories reinforce the approved narrative,” Moise said. “I lived through transition. I lived through detransition. I have every constitutional right to speak honestly about what happened to me and what I now believe.”

Moise is also openly Republican and has publicly expressed conservative political views.

“Government officials are free to disagree with me,” Moise said. “They can disagree with my politics. They can disagree with my views on gender. They can disagree with everything I say. What they cannot do is use government power to punish me for constitutionally protected speech.”

PRESERVATION AND THEME

Moise has begun seeking preservation and disclosure of records concerning the hiring and rescission process, including internal communications and records concerning her social-media activity, political views, detransition, and public advocacy - including any internet searches or forwarded posts about her in the ten days between acceptance and rescission.

The litigation is expected to examine Campanelli’s role in the rescission as well as the involvement of any other county officials or employees who participated in, recommended, approved, or influenced the decision.

“This case is not simply about losing a job,” Moise said. “It is about whether Americans have to censor their lawful political and social beliefs in order to work for their own government.”

For Moise, the case has taken on a simple theme: Hendrix v. Goliath.

“Goliath happens to be the government,” Moise said. “And the government answers to the Constitution.”

ABOUT THE PLAINTIFF AND THE FILING

Moise has practiced law in Michigan since 2011 and focuses her private practice on criminal defense. She is the principal of Black Letter Defense.

The lawsuit is expected to be filed in the United States District Court for the Western District of Michigan, Southern Division.

LEGAL DISCLAIMER

The claims described in this release are allegations. No court has yet determined that Muskegon County, Amy P. Campanelli, the State of Michigan, or any other prospective defendant violated Moise’s rights or otherwise acted unlawfully. Statements concerning Campanelli’s Cook County tenure are drawn from contemporaneous public reporting and official summaries, including the July 2023 Cook County Inspector General quarterly summary as reported by Injustice Watch and the Chicago Sun-Times; the 2020 Cook County Board approval of the Brown v. Cook County settlement; and the publicly filed complaint and January 7, 2022 memorandum opinion in Gill-Richards v. Campanelli, No. 20 C 00822 (N.D. Ill.). The Illinois ARDC closed its investigation of the Lawndale information-sharing matter in December 2023 without imposing discipline. Allegations in Gill-Richards are recited as allegations; that suit is not cited as a finding of liability. Nothing in this release is an accusation of an uncharged crime.

text:
🚨 NFL CAMP BUZZ  -  July 30  RAPID FIRE 🚨

🌵 Arizona Cardinals

- Tyler Allgeier / Jeremiyah Love
Tyler Allgeier said HC Mike LaFleur called him right after Jeremiyah Love was drafted and told him he envisions Allgeier and Love forming a strong tandem. Allgeier respected the communication.

- Michael Wilson
Mike LaFleur praised Wilson’s competitiveness, toughness, intelligence and work ethic, comparing parts of his profile to Puka Nacua and Robert Woods.

- Trey Benson / James Conner / Kendrick Bourne
Trey Benson is back practicing. James Conner is still out, but LaFleur said he is not concerned. Kendrick Bourne is operating as WR3.

🍑 Atlanta Falcons

- Bijan Robinson
Bijan was again on the field in a jersey, but no helmet or cleats, and did not practice.

- Brian Robinson Jr.
Brian Robinson returned to practice and got first-team carries after coming up gimpy the prior day.

- Falcons QB Health
Tua Tagovailoa returned to practice but only threw a few times in individual drills. Michael Penix Jr. did not throw Thursday on a scheduled rest day, with more rest days expected throughout camp.

- Falcons WR Structure
Drake London, Jahan Dotson, Olamide Zaccheaus and Zachariah Branch were discussed as the current WR structure: Dotson as WR2/outside capable, London slot-capable, Zaccheaus WR3 for now, and Branch likely starting as WR4/gadget with a chance to grow.

🐦‍⬛ Baltimore Ravens

- Ja’Kobi Lane
Lane had a strong day and got reps with Lamar Jackson. He made a leaping catch on a Lamar throw and is worth tracking alongside Sarratt and Devontez Walker.

- Lamar Jackson
Second straight locked-in day. Lamar was throwing dots and leading receivers at an elite level.

🦬 Buffalo Bills

- Josh Allen / DJ Moore
DJ Moore caught two TD passes from Josh Allen. Positive early signal that the connection is syncing up.

- DJ Moore Usage
Josh Allen talked about throwing to Moore, and the note says Buffalo may have Moore on the field nearly every down — possibly 80-90% of snaps, which would be elite usage and a departure from the prior WR-by-committee approach.

🐻 Chicago Bears

- Rome Odunze
Odunze walked back his “new normal” foot comments. He said his foot feels amazing, that he did not articulate it well, and that he is completely fine.

- Bears Camp Day 2
Massive day for Luther Burden, who was the most targeted receiver on the field. Caleb Williams looked great and completed the majority of his passes. Kyle Monangai was not seen on the field by media.

- Zavion Thomas
Zavion Thomas rotated in with the first team.

- Kalif Raymond
Raymond has been impressive since OTAs/minicamp and continued it in camp. He was described as quick, fast, shifty, reliable catching the ball, and the player of the day.

🐅 Cincinnati Bengals

- Chase Brown
Joe Burrow essentially described Chase Brown as an every-down back: he can protect, trains like a receiver, and does not need to come off the field. The takeaway is that his 2025 second-half role may carry into 2026.

🟤 Cleveland Browns

- Browns WR/QB Practice Note
Deshaun Watson looked brutal with back-to-back INTs while working with the first team. Shedeur Sanders was not great, but sounded better than Watson. Jerry Jeudy and Isaiah Bond were the first-team WRs. KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston worked with the second team.

- KC Concepcion / Denzel Boston
Todd Monken said rookies have to earn first-team reps, so the second-team usage should not be overread yet.

⭐ Dallas Cowboys

- Dak Prescott / CeeDee Lamb / George Pickens
Dak Prescott was sharp on Day 2. CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens had really good days.

- Jaydon Blue
Brian Schottenheimer said Blue needs to take the next step and believes he will. Blue understands his role.

- Ryan Flournoy
The special teams coach wants Flournoy to play special teams, but Schottenheimer does not want him to because he views him as a good WR. Strong internal signal for Flournoy.

🐴 Denver Broncos

- Jaylen Waddle
Broncos takeaway: Waddle had an insane one-handed catch in the end zone during individual drills.

🦅 Philadelphia Eagles

- DeVonta Smith
Smith beat Quinyon Mitchell for a second straight day. A great daily battle with a well-placed Jalen Hurts throw into good coverage.

- 12 Personnel / WR Usage
In 12 personnel, the Eagles used DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks at WR with Dallas Goedert and Johnny Mundt at TE. Makai Lemon and Hollywood Brown also worked with the first-team offense, though not necessarily in 12P.

- Tank Bigsby
Bigsby is getting a lot of early practice action. He ran in a TD, caught a ball over the middle from Jalen Hurts, and got a lot of reps while Saquon Barkley worked through run plays with new OC Sean Mannion.

- Jalen Hurts / Offense Structure
Hurts is under center most of the time with a lot of play action.

🧀 Green Bay Packers

- MarShawn Lloyd
Lloyd took some first-team reps. The team wants to keep building his workload during camp. Jordan Love called him a special playmaker. Chris Brooks is on NFI and was not practicing.

🐂 Houston Texans

- Woody Marks
DeMeco Ryans said the Texans see a second-year jump from Woody Marks: faster and making good decisions.

- Jaylin Noel
Noel hurt his finger catching passes. Nick Caserio said it happened three or four days ago, is short term, and they are not overly concerned. Expected to be a few weeks.

- Tank Dell
Nick Caserio said Dell probably has another week or so of work before getting on the practice field. The note says Dell and Noel’s timelines may end up close together.

🐆 Jacksonville Jaguars

- Chris Rodriguez
Rodriguez said the plan is to be back for Week 1, taking it step by step. Liam Coen emphasized it is a long camp and season, and they want him back without hiccups.

- Bhayshul Tuten
Tuten’s strong practices have been consistent across the offseason and early camp. The Jaguars defense has snuffed out many runs, but Tuten has been the exception, popping multiple big gains on back-to-back days.

- Tuten First-Team Reps
Tuten keeps getting first-team reps while Rodriguez is limited and is taking advantage of the window.

- Parker Washington
Washington was the star of Jaguars practice. He was a tough cover, got open over the middle with ease, and showed strong sideline chemistry with Trevor Lawrence.

- Parker Washington / Coen Praise
Liam Coen said Trevor Lawrence is probably throwing to Parker Washington and Brenton Strange the most among current roster players. Coen said he is confident in Washington and excited to see what he can do.

- Travis Hunter
Hunter’s 11-on-11 snap tracker was identical across two days: Day 1 had eight defensive snaps and four offensive snaps; Day 2 had eight defensive snaps and four offensive snaps.

🐏 Los Angeles Rams

- Puka Nacua
Puka has been “the star” of Rams camp and continues to develop as a downfield threat. By all accounts, he is destroying camp after his rehab stint, leading in catch volume and explosive plays.

🐬 Miami Dolphins

- De’Von Achane
Achane said the biggest difference in Bobby Slowik’s offense is a plan to be run-heavy. He added that his goal is to win the rushing title.

🧭 Minnesota Vikings

- J.J. McCarthy
Kevin O’Connell still sees long-term upside in McCarthy and wants him to keep developing into someone who can help them win games.

- Kyler Murray / J.J. McCarthy Day 2
Not a great Day 2 for Kyler outside of a couple throws. He got most first-team reps but had misses and botched snap exchanges. McCarthy had a second straight solid day with a high completion rate but lower average depth of target.

- Kyler Murray / Jordan Addison
Murray and Addison spent two months throwing together this offseason.

🇺🇸 New England Patriots

- TreVeyon Henderson / Rhamondre Stevenson Pass Pro
Mike Vrabel praised Rhamondre Stevenson’s pass protection and said TreVeyon Henderson is continuing to work on it. Current trust on pass downs appears to lean Stevenson.

- Rhamondre Stevenson Passing Game
Vrabel also mentioned opportunities for Rhamondre in the passing game when asked about A.J. Brown.

- Patriots WR Trade Possibility
Vrabel did not dismiss the idea of trading a WR, saying they are always looking to improve through draft capital, adding players, or keeping the guys they have.

- Kyle Williams / Boutte
Kyle Williams is off the initial 53-man roster projection. Boutte continues to impress and has been the offense’s best player while Brown and Doubs have started slow.

- Eli Raridon
Raridon is projected as TE2 on an early 53-man roster projection. Pads are not on yet, so that is the real test, but veteran TE signing whispers have dwindled.

⚜️ New Orleans Saints

- Chris Olave Extension
The Saints are signing Olave to a four-year extension worth up to $132M.

- Olave Medical/Contract Context
Jeff Mueller noted the timing makes sense because the Saints likely wanted to make sure Olave was cleared from the pulmonary embolism before offering $90M guaranteed. Big news for Olave and Tyler Shough.

🗽 New York Giants

- Malik Nabers
Nabers said there are no target dates for his return, but he feels good and wants to keep stacking days.

- Nabers Practice Participation
Nabers worked for the first 20 minutes of practice, participating in individual drills and routes on air. He looked sharp, watched a few periods, went inside midway through practice, then returned after practice to play catch with Jaxson Dart.

- Cam Skattebo
Skattebo was the first RB with the first team, as expected.

- Isaiah Likely
Likely got a ton of middle-of-field targets from Dart.

- Jaxson Dart / Giants Offense
Dart was heavily under center. Cam Skattebo and Darius Slayton were with the first-team offense as expected. Tyrone Tracy caught a pass from Dart, so he is also getting some first-team work.

 - Darius Slayton
Slayton stepped back in with the first-team offense after missing most of spring due to sports hernia surgery.

🐾 Carolina Panthers

- Chris Brazzell
Brazzell will undergo season-ending surgery for a torn LCL. The team and Brazzell view surgery as best for his future.

- Brazzell Fallout
Good news/bad news framing: bad for his rookie year and likely reduces Tetairoa McMillan’s slot increase; good long term because surgical repair may reduce instability concerns.

- Bryce Young
A Panthers observer note says Bryce Young’s practice performance may point toward a really good, possibly great season. The writer said a dazzling practice made him re-evaluate Young.

- J.T. Sanders
With Brazzell out, Sanders’ summer becomes bigger. In theory, his hybrid body could help free up slot usage, especially in red-zone 11 personnel looks. He had a slow start but a strong day yesterday.

- Jonathan Brooks
Brooks lined up wide and caught a contested deep ball down the sideline. His passing-game contributions could be fun if he stays healthy.

☠️ Las Vegas Raiders

- Raiders WR Rotation
Raiders continued rotating WRs. Tre Tucker, Jack Bech, Jalen Nailor, Dont’e Thornton Jr., and Benson all got reps with the 1s. It feels like Tucker and Nailor are ahead, with the rest trying to prove they can be dependable No. 3 options.

🟡 Pittsburgh Steelers

- Rico Dowdle / Jaylen Warren
Dowdle and Warren are splitting first-team reps. Dowdle got reps ahead of Warren today, the reverse of yesterday, but both worked with the first-team offense.

- Aaron Rodgers / Pat Freiermuth
Rodgers had a couple nice throws, including a tight-window dot to Freiermuth on an in-breaking route.

🌉 San Francisco 49ers

- Ricky Pearsall
The 49ers hoped Pearsall’s knee would heal on its own, but it is swelling two days into camp. Surgery is looking increasingly possible; if that happens, he would miss the full season.

- Pearsall Timeline / PT Note
Jeff Mueller would give it until the end of August because PCL recoveries can take 9-12 months, but surgery remains logical if the issue does not improve.

- De’Zhaun Stribling / WR Fallout
If Pearsall has PCL surgery, De’Zhaun Stribling rises as a name to draft/monitor. DeMarcus Robinson, Jacob Cowing, or a free-agent addition are also names to watch.

- Deebo Samuel Reunion
Deebo Samuel is signing back with the 49ers on a one-year deal worth up to $7M.

🌊 Seattle Seahawks

- Jadarian Price
Pretty definitive RB1 signal. Greg’s note says the lead RB on the first play of the first full-team scrimmage was Jadarian Price. Brian Fleury’s system seems to prioritize RB involvement in the passing game, and Sam Darnold mentioned Price and George Holani in that role.

🏴‍☠️ Tampa Bay Buccaneers

- Baker Mayfield Contract
The Bucs only offered Mayfield a two-year deal and were reportedly pretty far from the $50M/year range. Mayfield has closed contract talks until after the season and said if they waited this long, it is only going to get worse because he plans to have a big year.

- Mayfield Feeling Undervalued
Mayfield said he is thankful for the chance Tampa gave him, but he knows what he has brought leadership-wise and play-wise. He said it was disappointing to feel disrespected and undervalued.

- Bucky Irving
Irving took first-team reps and has no limitations, per Todd Bowles.

- Chris Godwin / Ted Hurst
Godwin was present but not participating. As a result, Ted Hurst got more time with the ones during individual drills.

⚔️ Tennessee Titans

- Titans Pass Catchers / Cam Ward Bonding Trip
Wan’Dale Robinson being highly targeted as a new WR is a positive. Ayomanor, Robinson and Tate were among players Cam Ward invited to Miami for a three-week bonding experience.

- Calvin Ridley
Ridley was not at the three-week bonding experience. The vibes are off, referencing prior reports about him battling for WR3 with Ayomanor/Dike and his 2025 performance drop-off.

🪖 Washington Commanders

- Jayden Daniels
Day 2 Commanders recap: Jayden looked way more comfortable.

- Commanders RB Room
The RB room was described as really talented.
