All right, so you’re starting off talking about “toughness” when I didn’t say anything about toughness, and right there you’re peeking through and showing what you’re actually upset about. What you’re upset about is that Kuminga would not acquiesce to a franchise you’re obsessed with, and you are completely blind to when it comes to judging their actions. First, you are absolutely wrong when you said the Lakers’ offer was no longer on the table. I’m not sure if you know how to read, but the report yesterday was that it was three years, close to $40 million. So they actually upped the offer from around $10 million a season to around $12 million a season, and JK still said no. So when you said they went back and the deal was gone, no, it wasn’t. And you’re also too stupid to understand that the Lakers used cap space to sign someone like Sandro. Do you really expect any self-respecting man or player to be told, “We want you to start, we want you to play heavy minutes, we want you taking difficult defensive assignments, but we’re going to pay you less than a guy who is most likely coming off the bench”? Would you do that in your own career? Would you work harder, longer, have more responsibility and more demand on your body while making less than somebody doing less? No, you wouldn’t. But when it comes to professional sports, you stop looking at these people like actual human beings making career decisions and start looking at them like toys who are supposed to do whatever makes your favorite franchise happy.

Now that your contract statement is out of the way, let’s also talk about the reports that he turned down offers from the Bulls and the Blazers. If you actually looked into it instead of speaking out of your ass, Chicago had its roughly $9 million room exception available and Portland had access to its full mid-level exception, around $15 million. So not only did he turn down the Lakers’ three-year offer starting around $12 million or more, he turned down roughly $9 million from Chicago and potentially around $15 million from Portland to choose Minnesota at around $6 million. Why would a player do that? Because there is a very fine line in this league between becoming what you believe you can become and falling into obscurity as another good player who gets paid but never becomes anything people really remember. Nicolas Batum, Harrison Barnes, Jerami Grant, good players, long careers, big paydays, but that clearly is not what Kuminga wants for himself. And you seem like the kind of person who doesn’t understand that kind of ambition because you don’t understand what it takes sometimes to fight for what you believe about yourself. Sometimes greatness requires sacrifice. Sometimes it requires giving up the safer money today because you believe the right opportunity can turn you into something much bigger tomorrow.

You brought up the difference between Castle and Harper, but Kuminga fans have already said plenty of times that it probably would have been better for him not to be drafted by Golden State. And you’re so caught up in being offended by that because you’re fearful of what happens if Kuminga now goes to Minnesota, the Wolves are near the top of the West, Golden State is looking up at them in the standings, and Kuminga is shining in exactly the kind of role he spent years asking for. Yes, the situations are different, that is the entire point. Kuminga was drafted seventh overall onto a dynasty championship team, which means he had to sit, wait and play a role while watching his peers, Jalen Green, Jalen Johnson, Cade Cunningham, Scottie Barnes, Alperen Sengun and others, get playing time, touches, development, money and accolades. Then someone like you comes along later and says, “Well, Kuminga isn’t as good as Cade Cunningham,” or “He isn’t Jalen Johnson.” You don’t know that because he was never allowed to find out. Jalen Johnson’s first three years were nothing compared to Jonathan Kuminga’s first three years, and Kuminga had to fight and claw through more shit just to get on the floor. Yet by Johnson’s fifth year he is an All-Star and All-NBA player because he was drafted to a team that was up and down, under .500, trying to figure out what it was, and therefore able to develop him. If Kuminga had been drafted into a situation like San Antonio, where they were 13th or 14th in the conference, developed their young players and then climbed into contention, he could very well be talked about in the same breath as the best players in his draft class right now. Would he already have a championship? Probably not. But his individual career would not have been stuck in this constant argument about whether he deserves 25 minutes, 30 minutes, touches or permission to make mistakes.

And this is where I can even be fair to Golden State. As a rookie, fine, they won a championship. I can understand limiting him. In his second season, they were defending the title. Fine, I can even understand some limitation then. But when Andrew Wiggins stepped away and Kuminga got his opportunity, that should have changed everything. A 20-year-old seventh overall pick goes out there in roughly 24 minutes a game and gives you around 14 points on 55% shooting and 44% from three, and in almost any normal organization that player is never getting buried again. That is the moment you say, “Our investment is starting to come to fruition, and now we need to make the roster work around that.” That is exactly how Draymond Green took David Lee’s spot. Opportunity opened, the younger player proved himself and the organization adjusted. So even if the second-year playoffs went exactly the same way, that offseason Golden State should have made moves to permanently open a path for Kuminga. Andrew Wiggins should have been traded. The dynasty was effectively over. The good vibes were gone. You failed in your title defense, Draymond Green punched Jordan Poole, the sixth man and an important part of the last championship, and instead of getting proper value for Poole, you sent an 18-point-per-game scorer, who had been around 20 during the championship season, to the Washington Wizards, basically the worst place you could send a player, for Chris Paul, who Washington was probably going to buy out anyway. And Golden State gave up Ryan Rollins and a first-round pick in the process. They needed frontcourt size and could have used that asset to address it, but instead they brought in another 6-foot guard and one of the Warriors’ biggest historical rivals to put next to Steph Curry.

The original logic was supposed to be that Chris Paul would stabilize the non-Steph minutes because Golden State’s starting five had actually been one of the best five-man units in basketball the year before. So fine, let Paul run the second unit. But then Kuminga’s third year comes and Draymond gets suspended for 17 games, Andrew Wiggins has the worst season of his career and is scoring around 13 points per game while still starting and playing about 27 minutes, Klay Thompson is declining, frustrated and chucking shots, and the roster construction is becoming a mess. Through all of that, one of the only real bright spots was Jonathan Kuminga fighting his way through it and averaging around 16 points on 52 to 53% shooting in only about 26 minutes per game, still behind Andrew Wiggins. He even had stretches where he was averaging around 25 and 7 over 7 games. Remember the Atlanta game where he goes 11/11 a Warriors record. That year he also broke the Warriors record for dunks and that's in 26mpg off the bench. Imagine what a show we would have gotten if the chains were off. Now to the Nuggets game 01-04-2024 Which was the game he finally said he lost faith in Kerr. Kuminga had 16, 4 and 4 on 5-of-7 shooting when Kerr took him out with 5:36 left in the third quarter. The Warriors had a 14-point lead when he sat. Kerr never put him back in the game because, in Kerr’s mind and in the minds of idiot fans like you, going back to the “championship guys” is always supposed to be the answer. Golden State lost by three. That is the kind of shit you people allowed yourselves to normalize.

And you are not really a Warriors fan if you cannot criticize that. You are a Steph Curry, Steve Kerr and dynasty-memory fan. You are loyal to the feeling those years gave you, and anything that challenges those people threatens that memory. That’s why you get offended by Kuminga wanting something different. If Kuminga had been drafted on almost any other rebuilding team, he probably would have been playing 32 to 36 minutes by age 20 or 21 and given permission to make mistakes, handle the ball, develop his reads and figure out exactly how good he could become. Instead, Golden State wanted him to play the Andrew Wiggins role without giving him Andrew Wiggins minutes, Andrew Wiggins touches, Andrew Wiggins freedom or the developmental runway Andrew Wiggins got before he ever became that player. They wanted him to come into games, don’t shoot threes, don’t use your midrange, don’t over-dribble, set screens, cut, defend and help somebody else’s greatness. Well, fuck that. Andrew Wiggins and Aaron Gordon got five or six years to find out whether they could be lead guys. They got the touches, the money and the contracts first. Wiggins got to find out in Minnesota that even with other talented players around him, being the number one guy was not going to lead to championship-level basketball. Aaron Gordon got to find out in Orlando that giving him more offensive responsibility still did not make him a franchise offensive star. Then they were able to accept complementary roles because they had already been given the experiment. Kuminga was being told to accept the conclusion without ever being given the experiment. <Read that last line again!

And while all of that was happening, other Warriors players were being given exactly the runway Kuminga was denied. Look at Brandin Podziemski. He has been allowed to miss passes, over-dribble, drive into traffic, get blocked, turn the ball over, go through long stretches of terrible shooting and still be played through it. When Steph missed time, Podziemski had stretches early where he was under 40% from the field and under 30% from three, yet Kerr kept giving him major minutes and starting opportunities because the organization believed in him. Do you honestly think Jonathan Kuminga would ever have been allowed to play 30 minutes per game as a starter while shooting under 40% and under 30% from three for that long without Kerr yanking him around? Of course not. That is what Kuminga fans mean by hypocrisy. And now you see it with Will Richard. Richard can score 30, come into a lineup, play well and help Golden State win, and then suddenly he is reduced or removed. When reporters ask Kerr why he isn’t playing more, the answer is basically, “Well, he’s a rookie.” Then why the fuck was being a rookie never a problem when Brandin Podziemski was a rookie? I watched games where Pat Spencer was playing better than Podziemski, where other guards came in and gave the team more energy, and Kerr would still force Podziemski back into the game even when he was having one of the worst games of anybody on the floor. The Warriors would have a lead, Podziemski would come back in, the lead would disappear, and Kerr would still stick with him. That is organizational faith. That is a developmental runway. Kuminga wanted the same thing.

That is also why the whole argument that Kuminga should have just stayed patient is ridiculous. Patient until when? Until he was 26? 27? Until Steph Curry retired? When exactly was the organization finally going to give him the same leash other high draft picks around the league get? Jalen Brown had flaws and Boston let him develop. Jalen Johnson had flaws and Atlanta let him develop. Everyone has flaws. Kuminga was supposed to keep waiting while Steph dragged one knee across the finish line and nobody even knows when that finish line is coming, while Draymond Green refuses to step down and spends the offseason podcasting, judging dunk contests and playing golf. And yes, I’ll say it now, I think Draymond is going to have one of the worst seasons of his career because from everything I’ve seen this offseason he looks out of shape. At what point does the organization finally say enough? We thought it would be after this past season when they won 37 games and now you have $50 to 55 million tied into one aging situation and another roughly $15 million potentially injured for half the following season. Even after trading Kuminga, I thought there was no way Steve Kerr would be back. Yet here we are again, Kerr extended another two years as the highest-paid coach in the league. Is he the best coach in the league? No. He might be the best coach for making Steph Curry comfortable in his twilight years and running an offense designed around helping Steph reach 30,000 points and go out with what they call dignity, but even Draymond has basically said success now can mean national TV games and sold-out arenas. That tells you what this is. They are not operating like a franchise whose only priority is winning championships anymore.

Steph Curry, Draymond Green and Steve Kerr have been corrupted by ego and by what I would call king syndrome. They became so important to the organization that everything started revolving around protecting their status, their comfort and their place in Warriors history, even if younger players got stepped on in the process. So sure, give Kerr more money. Extend Steph another two years for some massive 140 million dollar number. Give Draymond another two years and $40 million. You did it for Kristaps Porzingis too, and Kuminga outplayed Porzingis after that trade in meaningful basketball. And yes, someone like you will immediately say, “Well Porzingis scored more points.” I’m talking about total impact. Kuminga defended better, out rebounded, shot a higher percentage from the field and from three over that stretch, and while Porzingis could not make it through the second half of a play-in game, Kuminga became a major reason Atlanta won two playoff games against the eventual champions. When I say major reason, I mean across those two one-point wins he was the second-leading scorer, arguably their best defender and had the biggest plus-minus swing. Atlanta’s established starters were minus-13 across those two wins, while Kuminga himself was plus-13. That is a game-changing impact. Yet the Warriors can give $40 million to Porzingis and people act like Kuminga wanting opportunity and respect is some outrageous act of entitlement.

And that gets back to Minnesota. You act like his agent failed because he took $6 million. But again, he had other options. Portland had access to roughly $15 million through its mid-level exception. Chicago could offer around $9 million. The Lakers were reportedly around $12 million per year. So why choose Minnesota? Because Portland would have brought another complicated forward situation with Toumani Camara, Jerami Grant and other players who already view themselves as established. What happens when Shaedon Sharpe comes back? Now you are dealing with Dame, Ja Morant, Camara, Grant and their center rotation, and Kuminga is again fighting through an existing hierarchy. The same kind of issue happened in Atlanta. It wasn’t that Kuminga didn’t play well or didn’t buy into his role. The problem was that he threatened other people’s spots. He was a threat to Nickeil Alexander-Walker’s minutes, to Dyson Daniels’ role, to Jalen Johnson’s touches, to Onyeka Okongwu’s visibility, to CJ McCollum’s shine, and Atlanta also has developmental forwards like Asa Newell. Kuminga can smile, work out, show up and do everything professionally, but there are only so many NBA jobs and only five starting spots. There are even fewer starting spots where you are allowed to be more than a complementary player.

Minnesota offers something different. There is a clear spot, there is belief, there is no constant looking over his shoulder, and there is no weekly competition with some veteran who believes the job belongs to him because of seniority. Yes, Anthony Edwards and LaMelo Ball are ahead of him in the hierarchy, but I view them differently because LaMelo is a point guard. His touches can actually help a scorer like Kuminga. Steve Nash was never necessarily top three on his own teams in scoring, but he controlled the offense. So you can say Ant is the number one option, LaMelo is the number two in the offensive hierarchy and Kuminga is the number three, but LaMelo could still average fewer points than Kuminga because those are different jobs. And we already know what Kuminga can do without plays being run for him. His career per-36 scoring is over 20 points per game. We have seen him in heavier roles put up around 26 points per game for stretches. We have seen him start while not really being an offensive option at all and still give you 17 to 20 simply by running the floor, cutting, getting putbacks, catching lobs, attacking openings and taking whatever shots happen to come to him. So what happens when a coach says, “Tonight Kuminga has an advantage. Let’s actually call four or five plays for him”? Run a pick-and-roll. Give him an isolation. Let him attack a mismatch. Put the ball in his hands and let him make a decision. I’m saying it is a 48-minute game. You can actually devote a handful of possessions to using one of your most talented players to what they do best.

So in a lot of ways, this is Kuminga starting his career over. This is his rookie year. This is the chance he has been asking for. And yes, he is taking less money to get it. That is why this is not about his agent failing and it is not about Kuminga being obsessed with money. If it were about money, he made the wrong decision. He literally rejected more money. It is about the dream. It is about finding out what he actually is. And that only happens with a healthy season as a starter playing 30-plus minutes per game, not constantly going in and out of the lineup because someone ahead of him got hurt, someone came back, someone had a personal issue, or the coach suddenly decided he didn’t like the fit. That is what people miss when they say, “Well, just play the Aaron Gordon role.” Aaron Gordon got years to prove whether he could be more. Andrew Wiggins got years to prove whether he could be more. Then they became highly paid complementary pieces. Kuminga was being asked at 21, 22, 23 years old to surrender the possibility of ever finding out.

And yes, Lakers mishandled the situation. I think the Hawks played their own role in making the market difficult, and I think the Lakers were arrogant in believing that if they squeezed the market enough, eventually Kuminga would have no choice but to come to Los Angeles because “we’re the Lakers.” Their actions basically said, “Come here, be our little tool. We’ll pay Sandro more than you even though you’re going to play more. We’ll ask you to take the hardest defensive assignments. We’ll ask you to rotate behind Luka and Reaves when they get blown by. We’ll put wear on your body guarding bigger players. And offensively, stand in the corner, catch lobs, take layups and be grateful that you’re complementing somebody else’s greatness.” Why should he accept that? Because it’s Los Angeles? Because they have banners? They had cap space and decided how they wanted to use it. Fine. Stand on that. You wanted Grimes? Stand on that. You wanted Sandro? Stand on that. You wanted to overpay Kessler after he missed an entire season and his previous seasons had not shown enough to justify that kind of payday? Stand on that. But don’t then turn around and act insulted because Kuminga refuses to take less money than players Lakers prioritized while carrying a bigger workload.

And the last part is the biggest thing you don’t understand. This isn’t really about a contract. This is about a person deciding what kind of career he wants to have. Maybe he goes to Minnesota, averages 18, 7 and 3, they make the second round or Western Conference Finals and he never makes an All-Star team. Fine. Then at least he took the chance. But imagine if by the end of 2027 Jonathan Kuminga is a one-time All-Star, an All-Defensive selection and a two-time NBA champion. Then every sacrifice was worth it, and the entire narrative changes. Could it go the other way? Of course. But that is for him to find out. That is what life is, taking chances. He has a dream, just like Kobe had a dream, just like Michael Jordan had a dream, and before you twist that into something stupid, I am not saying Kuminga is Kobe Bryant or Michael Jordan. I am talking about mentality. Players get told no. Players get told to wait their turn. Kobe himself had established players in front of him and a coach who did not initially want to give him the opportunity he believed he deserved, even while he was destroying people in practice. Kuminga has had Andre Iguodala telling you how physically extraordinary he was at 19, Jimmy Butler telling you how talented he is and how much more advanced Kuminga was at those ages than Butler himself had been. Yet Jimmy Butler eventually got 35 to 36 minutes a night in Chicago at those ages. Iguodala was playing nearly 40 minutes early in Philadelphia at those ages. Kuminga has spent years fighting to play over 25mpg!

You can never give those years back to him. You can give him another contract. You can give him more money. You cannot make him 20/21 years old again. That is why he is taking the $6 million now. He has a clear spot, a team that believes in him, a chance to remain relevant, a chance to put up numbers, a chance to be near the top of the Western Conference and maybe make a championship run. More importantly, he finally gets the chance to find out whether what he believes about himself is true. Maybe it is. Maybe it isn’t. But he deserves the chance to find out, and he was never going to get that by sitting around waiting for Steph Curry, Draymond Green, Steve Kerr and an organization obsessed with preserving the past to finally decide when his life could begin. So no, I don’t blame his agent, and I don’t blame Kuminga. I blame bad organizational management, years of inconsistent standards and an agenda that repeatedly punished one player for wanting more while giving other players far more room to fail.

That’s the difference between you and him. You would rather take the safe path, accept whatever place somebody gives you and tell yourself you should be grateful. He would rather take the chance, climb the mountain and find out what is actually on the other side. He may fail. He may succeed. But at least he is willing to fight for the possibility of becoming what he believes he can become, because that is the difference between your name being remembered when you are gone and your name disappearing like you were never here. You can be the kid in Troy who is too afraid to go fight the mountain of a man and stays home, or you can be Achilles and go face him. Because what you do in life echoes through eternity, and whether your name is remembered or forgotten depends on whether you were willing to take that chance.

text:
Amy Klobuchar Wants to Be Governor. Minnesota Should Ask Why.
Chapter 3 of 4: The Theory of the Trust Collapse
KLOBUCHAR Series — Part 3 of 4
Definitional Anchor
Chapters 1 and 2 established what happened: Minnesota built an unusually centralized, unusually generous fiscal and social architecture in 1971, and that architecture was systematically exploited for hundreds of millions of dollars across CCAP, Feeding Our Future, and a cluster of Medicaid, housing, and grant-administration programs. This chapter asks why the system was vulnerable in the first place, using two academic frameworks that surfaced in research on this subject, and traces how the state legislature responded to the fraud crisis — not by tightening the safety net, but by expanding it.
Elazar's Moralistic Political Culture
Political scientist Daniel J. Elazar divided American state political cultures into three types: individualistic, traditionalistic, and moralistic. Minnesota is widely considered the textbook moralistic case; Elazar himself called it "the epitome of the moralistic political culture," "more so than any other in the Union." In that culture, government is treated as a commonwealth instrument for the public good, politics as a civic duty rather than a marketplace, and corruption as a moral offense rather than an expected cost of doing business.
Elazar traced the pattern to settlement history: Yankee descendants of New England Puritans moved west through upstate New York and the Upper Midwest carrying a "holy commonwealth" idea of politics, reinforced by Scandinavian immigration. The result, in the standard account of the typology, was issue-oriented parties, high turnout, and policy innovation even without immediate electoral payoff — a bloc that includes Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa, the Dakotas, and much of New England and the Pacific Northwest.
That culture is why 1971 was possible. An individualistic state treats government as a transaction among interests; a traditionalistic state treats it as a device for maintaining existing hierarchies. A moralistic state treats a 157- to 159-day special session, a $580 million tax increase, a 23 percent jump in the state budget, and a regional tax-base-sharing statute derided as "Metropolitan Socialism" as a moral project: equalize school opportunity, cut the property-tax burden on homes and farms, and make the metropolis function as one fiscal community. Governor Wendell Anderson faced a Conservative-controlled legislature; the regular session failed; the special session that began May 25, 1971, and adjourned October 30 remains the longest in Minnesota history. The state assumed 65 percent of school operating costs, up from 43 percent. Almost every district saw property-tax relief; taxpayers as a whole paid more. The package became known as the Minnesota Miracle.
The Minnesota Fiscal Disparities Act of 1971 — formally the Charles R. Weaver Metropolitan Revenue Distribution Act — pooled 40 percent of the growth since 1971 in commercial, industrial, and public-utility tax base across the seven-county Twin Cities region and redistributed it by a formula favoring jurisdictions with lower fiscal capacity per capita. In Village of Burnsville v. Onischuk, 222 N.W.2d 523 (Minn. 1974), the Minnesota Supreme Court reversed a trial court that had struck the Act down under the state constitution's uniformity clause, treating the region as a legitimate single economic unit and allowing tax-base sharing to become a permanent fixture. The pool still operates, sharing on the order of $620 million in tax capacity annually in recent years.
The same cultural stock shows up in social-capital research. Robert Putnam's Comprehensive Social Capital Index — fourteen state-level indicators covering community organizational life, public-affairs engagement, volunteerism, informal sociability, and social trust, drawn from the General Social Survey, Roper, and DDB Needham Life Style surveys spanning the late 1970s through mid-1990s — ranked Minnesota third or fourth nationally depending on the specific published version of the table, clustered tightly with the Dakotas, Vermont, Montana, Nebraska, and Iowa. A more recent Joint Economic Committee Social Capital Index, built on 2010–2016 data across seven sub-indices including Community Health, Institutional Health, and Philanthropic Health, ranks Minnesota second nationally, trailing only Utah — a different instrument and a different decade, not a contradiction of Putnam's older finding, but corroboration that the underlying pattern persisted for decades. Cultural geographer Colin Woodard's regional mapping places Minnesota within "Yankeedom" and the "Midlands," blocs he characterizes by aggressive communitarianism and a belief that public goods require investment to let the majority thrive.
The through-line from Chapter 1 is direct. A moralistic culture builds large, trust-based systems with light verification because demanding heavy verification of neighbors is itself a violation of the communal ethic the system requires. That is a strength while the underlying trust holds. It is a structural weakness the moment a critical mass of claimants, vendors, or administrators decide not to honor it. Elazar's moralistic type "eschews corruption." It does not automatically detect corruption when the cheaters learn the forms, hire the right lawyers, and accuse the monitors of bias.
High institutional trust also delays the political response. In an individualistic culture, program abuse is expected and budgeted for — audits, match rates, built-in suspicion. In a moralistic culture, the first instinct is that the program is good and the critics are ungenerous. Oversight is treated as a second, separable task to be added later, rather than as the price of the benefit itself.
The Amy Chua Framework, Inverted
In World on Fire: How Exporting Free Market Democracy Breeds Ethnic Hatred and Global Instability (2003), legal scholar Amy Chua examined the volatile intersection of markets, democratization, and ethnic disparity, centered on the "market-dominant minority" — an ethnic minority that, under market conditions, controls a disproportionate share of a nation's private wealth. Markets concentrate wealth in the minority; democracy empowers the poorer majority; the result is backlash against markets, against democracy, or against the minority itself.
Applied to Minnesota, the paradigm inverts. The native-born, predominantly white majority remains the economically dominant demographic and the principal funder of the tax base. Rapidly grown immigrant and refugee populations — including the nation's largest Somali-American community, concentrated in the Twin Cities — are, on average, the more economically marginalized class. Minnesota does not use laissez-faire markets as the integration device; it uses a highly interventionist, high-trust welfare and nonprofit apparatus — progressive taxation, refundable credits, Medicaid waivers, child-care subsidies, nutrition sponsors, housing-stabilization vendors — extracting wealth from the dominant tax base and redistributing it through programs that are, by design, easy to enter and hard to watch in real time.
Where Chua's traditional model generates friction because the market itself widens visible ethnic inequality, the Minnesota model generates friction when the redistributive apparatus is perceived to be compromised. A moralistic culture requires unusually high civic trust to justify its tax burden. When that trust breaks, resentment is disproportionate to the dollars charged in any single indictment, because the injury is not only fiscal — it is the accusation that the commonwealth ethic was naive.
Public charging documents and reporting on the nutrition, housing, autism, and related cases show a large share of defendants drawn from Minnesota's Somali-American networks, a fact the U.S. Attorney's Office has stated in open court. That fact does not license collective blame. Most members of the community are not defendants; many are citizens; a substantial share were born in the United States. The analytical point is narrower: a high-trust system with weak site inspection, self-attested enrollment, and rapid pandemic-era waiver of ordinary controls is especially exploitable by any tight network that learns the reimbursement rules. Networks exist in every ethnicity. The state's error was assuming that moralistic norms would travel automatically with the money.
Whether or not one accepts Chua's framework as a complete explanation, the mechanism is visible in Minnesota's present politics. When a majority that funds a redistributive system concludes the system is being plundered rather than used as intended, the backlash targets not only the people charged but the legitimacy of the programs themselves — and, indiscriminately, whole communities associated with the caseloads. That is the weather any governor inherits, and specifically the weather Klobuchar must navigate: she is a moralistic-party nominee asking for executive power after the trust that underwrote the model cracked on her party's watch.
How Trust Became a Control System
The Office of the Legislative Auditor has said in plain language what the culture made easy to miss. A February 2023 OLA review found "pervasive noncompliance" by state agencies with grant-management policies and little statutory authority to force compliance; state-funded grants to nonprofits had grown from $389 million in 2018 to $558 million in 2022. A January 2026 OLA review of the DHS Behavioral Health Administration — already documented in Chapter 2 — found the identical posture on a smaller stage: money out the door, rules on paper, enforcement optional, staff caught backdating documents once the audit began.
The June 2024 special review of MDE's oversight of Feeding Our Future concluded MDE "failed to act on warning signs known to the department prior to the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic," "did not effectively exercise its authority to hold Feeding Our Future accountable," and "was ill-prepared to respond." Parallel programs repeated the shape: a small, well-intended benefit, explosive claim growth, delayed shutdown. Housing Stabilization Services moved from a low-single-digit-million projection to more than $100 million before Minnesota closed it in October 2025. EIDBI autism spending rose from hundreds of thousands of dollars in 2018 toward hundreds of millions by the mid-2020s. CCAP has the longest prehistory of all: a 2016 HHS-OIG audit found a high improper-payment rate; a 2019 OLA review could prove only $5–6 million in fraud for 2013–2018 but believed the true figure was higher; a 2025 federal sample of 2023 CCAP payments still found an 11 percent documentation-error rate.
Light verification was not an accident. It was the operational expression of moralistic trust. Site counts no inspector could reconcile with building capacity, meal claims implying thousands of children in empty rooms, autism caseloads scaling faster than any plausible incidence change, housing vendors billing for services that left clients unhoused — each required someone in a state agency to say no to a claimant who could accuse the agency of racism, delay, or hostility to the poor. Feeding Our Future sued MDE and obtained court pressure that, auditors and prosecutors later argued, chilled enforcement. That is how a high-trust culture is gamed: not only by false invoices, but by turning the culture's own fairness norms into a shield.
A system that cannot say no without a federal search warrant is not generous. It is ungoverned. The moralistic claim was that Minnesota could run a bigger safety net because Minnesotans would not loot it. The last five years are the falsification of that claim at scale.
Doubling Down: The 2023 Tax Reform
By the 2023 legislative session the fraud was no longer a rumor. FBI raids on Feeding Our Future occurred in January 2022; indictments rolled through that fall; CCAP's problems were already a matter of legislative and media record. The DFL held the House, Senate, and governor's office and faced a historic surplus, commonly cited at about $17.5 billion for the planning cycle. It did not retreat from the 1971 redistributive ideal. It used the surplus to enact one of the most generous state-level family tax packages in the country, while also imposing new burdens on high-income and investment income.
HF1938 restructured family subsidies. Before 2023, Minnesota offered a Working Family Credit analogous to the federal EITC, phased in with earnings. The overhaul created a fully refundable Child Tax Credit of $1,750 per qualifying child under 18, with no cap on the number of children, plus an additional $350 base credit per family and scaled credits for dependents ineligible for the federal CTC. Combined credits phase out at 12 percent of income above $35,000 for married joint filers and $29,500 for others. The Department of Revenue reported that in the first year more than 215,000 returns claimed the child credit for more than 437,000 children.
PolicyEngine's microsimulation projected a static cost of about $444 million, a 1.9 percent reduction in overall poverty under the Supplemental Poverty Measure, a 9.4 percent reduction in child poverty, and a 45.6 percent reduction in deep child poverty. Standard and itemized deductions were sharply reduced for high earners — 10 percent reduction above $304,970 in AGI, 80 percent above $1 million — and a 1 percent tax on net investment income over $1 million took effect in 2024. On the corporate side, HF1938 restricted the Net Operating Loss deduction to 70 percent of taxable income (versus the federal 80 percent) and slashed Dividends Received Deduction percentages. The bill also expanded the Social Security income subtraction and created a new Retirement Benefits Subtraction for public pensions, aimed at slowing middle-class retiree out-migration.
The timing is the point. The state expanded refundable, largely self-attested benefits at the same moment its auditors and federal investigators were documenting systemic fraud in existing benefits. A fully refundable per-child credit with no cap on family size is not identical to a meal-site reimbursement. It is structurally similar in the way that matters for integrity: the claimant attests, the state pays, and the incentive to inflate the count of qualifying children rises with every additional $1,750. Legitimate anti-poverty effects and fraud risk are not opposites. They are the same instrument used by different people.
The Department of Revenue built the new credit's advance-payment mechanism, under Minn. Stat. § 290.0661, Subd. 8, with materially tighter controls than CCAP or Feeding Our Future ever had: a taxpayer must elect advance payment on a timely filed initial return, an amended return or audit disqualifies the election, and any overpayment is immediately added back to the taxpayer's liability with penalties. That is a real, deliberate pivot toward automated, reconciled, harder-to-game distribution — worth crediting, because it shows the state does know how to build a tighter system when it wants to. It also throws into relief how loose the nutrition and Medicaid pipelines were allowed to remain in parallel.
The legislature also moved, in 2023, to break up the sprawling DHS portfolio itself: the Department of Children, Youth and Families was created as a new cabinet-level agency consolidating childcare and family programs previously scattered across DHS, MDE, and Public Safety, with full implementation set for July 2025 — the same administrative reorganization documented in Chapter 2.
Expanding a benefit and tightening its verification were treated as separate problems, assigned to separate sessions, staffed by separate offices. Elazar's moralistic official believes the first duty is to enact the good; the second duty — to assume some recipients will lie — feels like a betrayal of the first. Whether that sequencing can survive contact with the last five years is the question the next governor answers in practice, not in press releases.
Klobuchar's own campaign now advertises distance from Walz: a first-day audit, a "plan to tackle fraud," "results, not excuses." As Hennepin County Attorney (1999–2007) she cultivated a tough-on-crime brand, including white-collar and tax cases, and has cited that record as proof she does not "like fraud or waste in government." That history is real. So is the fact that the programs now in ruins were expanded, waived, and under-audited while she was Minnesota's senior senator, not a powerless bystander. Chapter 4 takes up the personnel. The theoretical point belongs here: a prosecutor's temperament is not the same thing as a governor's willingness to shrink a moralistic state until it can be verified.
What "Trust Collapse" Means Operationally
Trust collapse is not a mood. It is a change in the cost of governing. When citizens believe benefits are mostly reaching the intended poor, they will tolerate high taxes and high caseloads. When they believe a non-trivial share is being converted into luxury vehicles, real estate, and overseas transfers — the pattern alleged and, in many Feeding Our Future cases, proved — they stop distinguishing the worthy recipient from the program. Legislators then face a trap: tighten rules and get accused of cruelty; leave rules loose and get accused of being marks.
Minnesota's 2023 choice was to spend the surplus on expansion first. Subsequent years have been spent on raids, sentences, program shutdowns, and campaign promises to audit later. That sequence is the moralistic reflex under pressure. It is also why "hundreds of millions" understates the political damage. Housing Stabilization Services no longer exists for the people it was written to serve — that is a deadweight loss no restitution order captures. Every honest clinic and daycare now operates under a cloud created by the dishonest ones. The culture that prided itself on being "intolerant of corruption" outsourced that intolerance to the FBI.
A governor who wants to rebuild the commonwealth has to do the thing the culture finds vulgar: treat verification as part of the benefit, not as an insult to the beneficiary. Identity, attendance, medical necessity, site capacity, beneficial ownership of vendors, and cross-program billing have to be matched in something close to real time. That is expensive. It is less expensive than another $243 million nutrition hole or another Medicaid waiver that has to be abolished because it became a business model.
Forward Tie-Line
Chapter 4 turns from theory to the people responsible for the system this chapter has described: Governor Tim Walz, whose administration oversaw both the fraud years and the 2023 expansion; Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan, who has moved on to a different ballot; Attorney General Keith Ellison, whose office held pieces of state-level enforcement; and Amy Klobuchar, the former Hennepin County prosecutor and now the DFL nominee for governor, asking Minnesotans to trust her with the job of fixing what her predecessors — and her own long tenure in the state's senior federal seat — did not.
The theory of the trust collapse is not that Minnesota was uniquely wicked. It is that Minnesota was uniquely certain it was good, and designed a fiscal machine that worked only if that certainty was true. The machine is still running. The certainty is not.

Bernie. Senator Sanders. My man.

This is the finest post you have ever written, and I mean that sincerely. You just published the single most devastating indictment of government economic intervention in modern American history, and you did it believing it was an argument FOR more government. You are living proof that God has a sense of humor.

Standing ovation. Truly. Now let me show you what you actually posted, because I do not think anybody on your staff ran it past a calculator. Or a person. Or a calculator operated by a person.

THE MATH YOU LEFT OUT

One 1973 dollar equals $7.52 today. That is BLS, not Bski. I know arithmetic is the enemy here, but ride with me.

Healthcare, $441 becomes $3,317. You listed $15,474. Real increase, 4.7x.

Home, $35,500 becomes $267,010. You listed $475,400. Real increase, 1.8x.

Rent, $133 becomes $1,000. You listed $2,017. Real increase, 2x.

Tuition, $514 becomes $3,866. You listed $11,950. Real increase, 3.1x.

Still bad. I am not pretending otherwise, and nobody is throwing a parade. But the gap between what you posted and what is true is wide enough to drive a bus through, and you were counting on nobody looking.

You posted raw nominal figures with no deflator, to an audience you assumed could not run the conversion. That is not economics, Senator. That is muddying the water to make it look deep.

YOUR CLOSING QUESTION, ANSWERED

"Has your income kept up?"

Median household income, 1973: $10,500. Census Bureau, report P60-96.

Median household income, latest: $83,730. Census Bureau.

That is a 697 percent increase. General prices rose 652 percent over the identical window. Income WON. By forty-five points. That number was one search away, which apparently was one search too many.

So the honest answer is YES. Median income slightly outran overall inflation. It simply failed to outrun the four categories you hand-picked, and you cling to those four the way a drunkard clings to a lamppost. For support, not for illumination.

THE QUESTION YOU CAREFULLY DID NOT ASK

What do healthcare, housing, rent, and college tuition have in common? Take your time. I have been grading freshman biology for a decade; I am comfortable with silence.

They are the four most subsidized, most regulated, most government-saturated markets in the United States. Every single one. Sometimes the majority just means all the fools are on the same side.

Meanwhile televisions, computers, toys, software, clothing, and cell service, the sectors Washington mostly left alone, collapsed in real price. Televisions are down roughly 97 percent since 2000. Funny how the stuff Congress never touched got cheaper. Almost like there is a pattern here, visible from space, waving a flag.

Government touches it, price explodes. Government keeps its hands off, price falls. Fifty-three years, same country, same currency, same workers. If your model cannot explain that, your model has a leak in the think tank.

That is not a talking point. That is a controlled experiment, and you are standing in the smoking crater of your own hypothesis requesting a larger appropriation. This is high-IQ stupid. Brilliant man. Not a lick of sense.

Quinn's First Law of Liberalism: liberalism always generates the exact opposite of its stated intent. You proved it with four data points and a rhetorical question. All foam, no beer.

AND WHY, EXACTLY, 1973?

Bold pick. Let me guess what Washington does next. Congress severs the dollar from gold entirely and hands itself an unlimited printing press... wait, I am being told they already did that. August fifteenth, 1971. Fully floating by March 1973. You chose the first clean year of the pure fiat dollar as your baseline, which is a bit like dating the fire from the moment somebody hid the extinguisher.

What is next, Senator? Congress rebuilds all of American medicine around third-party payment so that no patient ever sees a price again... wait, they already did THAT one too. Health Maintenance Organization Act of 1973. Signed December 29, 1973. He is more confused than a chameleon in a bag of Skittles.

You picked the crime scene and labeled it the control group. Your thesis has more holes than a screen door on a submarine in a hurricane.

COLLEGE: YOU SUBSIDIZED IT INTO ORBIT

The Education Amendments of 1972 created the federal grant that became Pell. Federal aid expanded for fifty years afterward, and tuition followed it like a shadow. Faster than green grass through a goose.

Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Staff Report 733: every additional dollar of subsidized federal student loan capacity passed through into higher tuition at roughly SIXTY CENTS ON THE DOLLAR. That is the Fed. Not a podcast. Not me. And I am glad you are not letting education get in the way of your ignorance on it.

You handed colleges a blank check drawn on the signature of eighteen-year-olds, and colleges cashed it. Now the proposed fix is more of the exact thing that broke it, a solution ranking somewhere between an inflatable dartboard and a cordless extension cord.

Light travels faster than sound. This is why some people appear bright until they speak.

HOUSING AND RENT: ALSO YOU

Single-family-only zoning. Minimum lot sizes. Parking minimums. Environmental review that turns a duplex into a six-year lawsuit. Then a decade of near-zero rates flooding a supply-starved market with cheap money. Every one of those was sold as help, and every one made it worse, which at this point is less a policy record than a magic trick performed by a man who cannot find his own shadow on a sunny day.

Also, median new home 1973: about 1,525 square feet. Today: over 2,200, with central air, multiple bathrooms, and an attached garage. You are comparing a Pinto to a Tahoe and billing the difference to greed. You can put lipstick on that pig. It is still a pig.

Want cheaper rent? Legalize building. That is the entire policy, it costs the taxpayer nothing, and that is precisely why it will never interest you. Clouds without rain. All promise, no delivery. Jude 12. Proverbs 25:14.

HEALTHCARE: SENATOR, YOU VOTED FOR THIS

Everybody reading, sit with this one, because it is the whole ballgame and they are counting on you skimming past it.

The ACA COVID subsidies were written as TEMPORARY in the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021, then extended as TEMPORARY in the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022. NOT ONE Republican voted for either bill. You voted for BOTH, @BernieSanders. You set the expiration date yourself, with your own hand, which makes the outrage about as credible as a handshake agreement with a used-car salesman.

Then your party shut the government down for 43 days demanding them back, which was a public confession, on the record, that a law named the AFFORDABLE Care Act is not affordable without emergency pandemic cash. The new CR passed. The government is open. That confession is still sitting in the transcript, and no press release is going to sand it off. They lie like fish swim.

Translated into plain English: "Last December my boss gave me a $1,000 bonus. This December he did not. Therefore he cut my pay and he is heartless." Take that argument to an actual employer and report back. Whoever drafted it could not pour water out of a boot with the instructions printed on the heel, and as a policy position it is about as useful as a solar-powered flashlight.

And why are YOU the loudest defender of routing every American through a government-guaranteed insurance conglomerate, rather than Health Savings Accounts and real price transparency, where the patient holds the dollar and the provider competes for it? Your side lit candles for Luigi Mangione over his hatred of that industry. Now you are its most reliable revenue stream. Pick a lane. You have more positions than a yoga instructor and less spine than a jellyfish.

Trying to reason with this is like trying to baptize a cat.

WHAT HAVE YOU ACTUALLY DELIVERED?

Sworn in January 1991. Thirty-five years in Congress. Congresswebsitee lists over four hundred bills you led as primary sponsor. THREE became law. Two of them renamed post offices in Vermont. Four hundred swings, three contacts, two of them buildings that already existed.

He has been in Congress so long the only thing he has passed is gas.

The brain is an amazing organ. It starts working in the womb and does not stop until you get elected to Congress.

Thirty-five years of this exact post. Same slides, new dates. Delusions of adequacy dressed up as a movement. And every one of those four lines got WORSE on your watch, in a chamber you sat in, on votes you personally cast. At what point does the diagnosis become the prescription, Senator? At what point do we admit the fire marshal keeps showing up smelling like gasoline?
THE PART ABOUT YOUR HOUSES

You own three homes while lecturing me about housing prices. Some hogs have all four feet and their snout in the trough.

So here is my standing offer, and it applies to every millionaire in that chamber hollering about the rich. Before the next "tax the rich" post, voluntarily remit DOUBLE what the IRS says you owe. Standard deduction only. No itemizing. No carve-outs, no foundations, no trusts, no clever accountant in Burlington. Publish the return. Until somebody does that, the sermon is a gray sprinkle on a rainbow cupcake.

Lead by example and I will sit through the whole homily. Until then it is a snollygoster selling indulgences, and the people who wrote the loopholes are the same people using them. All hat and no cattle.

WHILE WE ARE COUNTING OTHER PEOPLE'S MONEY

Every proposal you have ever floated arrives with the same page torn out. The one that says who pays. Medicare for All. Free college. Universal this, guaranteed that. Trillions in promises and never once a figure that survives contact with a calculator. If we discovered life on Mars, your caucus would try to send it money.

We have not had a real budget since Moby Dick was a minnow. There is always money for the next program and never a nickel to fix the last one, and somehow that is everyone's fault except the fault of the men who wrote it. Enough money to burn a wet mule, and not one dollar of accountability attached to any of it.

MY OWN MODEST PROPOSAL

Since price is apparently just a policy choice, allow me one. Mandatory GPA redistribution. Every student above a 3.5 surrenders points to every student below a 2.0. Everyone graduates. Nobody left behind. This is not a radical idea. It is just common sense, and I say that with a straight face, which is more than your last budget resolution managed.

While we are at it, free ice cream every Monday, and the store simply eats the cost. Also common sense. If stupidity were a renewable resource, this chamber would have solved the energy crisis in 1974.

We cannot run the greatest economy in human history on fairy dust and unicorn urine. Apparently we can run a gradebook on it. If that struck you as blatherskite, congratulations, you have now audited my entire objection to your economics.

CONGRESSIONAL RECORD, JANUARY 10, 1963

Rep. A.S. Herlong Jr. read 45 Communist Goals into the permanent record. Goal 17: get control of the schools and use them as transmission belts for socialism. Goal 32: support any socialist movement giving centralized control over education, social agencies, and welfare programs. Goal 40: discredit the family as an institution. Read that list, then read your platform, and tell me it is a coincidence with a straight face.

I am not asking anybody to believe in a conspiracy. I am asking them to grade the outcomes. That is what a science teacher does. A mountebank peddles the intention. A scientist checks the result.

Quinn's Sixth Law: facts are the enemy of liberalism. Quinn's Twenty-Fifth: liberals are great at giving away other people's money. Both were on full display in your original post, and neither one required a single assist from me. I just held up the mirror.

You speak an infinite deal of nothing, Senator. Shakespeare said it first, and he said it better.

ONE LAST THING, BECAUSE IT MATTERS

Wages are not decreed. They are agreed. Two free people shake hands. An employer offers, a worker accepts or walks, and if nobody accepts, the employer raises the offer or closes the doors. That is not exploitation, that is arithmetic, and treating it as villainy is a Billy-goat brain attached to a mockingbird mouth.

Price labor above what it produces and the least-skilled worker does not receive a raise. He receives a locked door. No first job, no resume, no rung one, and a lifetime of dependency he will vote to protect, because he is rational and you engineered his only rational choice. That is not compassion. That is a trap with a ribbon on it.

Every party that ever needed an underclass called it something noble. The antebellum South called it care. Jim Crow called it order. Yours calls it compassion. Same architecture, better branding, and in a battle of wits your economics would show up unarmed.

You cannot fix stupid. But you can vote it out of office.

But what do I know. I am only a high school science teacher, a medically retired Army combat medic, and a man who ran the deflator before he posted the chart.

Freddy, ten tailgates, and one piece of advice up front. Stick to the South. That is where this sport is a religion rather than a hobby.

1. THE GROVE, OLE MISS. This is the must. Not a suggestion, a must. Ten acres of oak trees, chandeliers hanging in tents, women in dresses, men in bow ties, bourbon at nine in the morning. And this year LSU comes to Oxford on September 19, Lane Kiffin against his old team. If you plan the whole trip around one date, make it this one.

2. RED RIVER RIVALRY. Texas versus Oklahoma, October 10, Cotton Bowl, Dallas. The stadium sits inside the State Fair of Texas, already on your list. Same day. Ride the DART in, eat a Fletcher's corny dog, watch a stadium split exactly down the fifty.

3. LSU NIGHT GAME, BATON ROUGE. Death Valley after dark is the loudest building in the sport and the food is the best tailgate food in America. Jambalaya, boudin, whole hogs, gumbo pots the size of bathtubs. Strangers will feed you because you are foreign. Say yes.

4. VOL NAVY, TENNESSEE. Knoxville. People tailgate from boats moored on the river behind the stadium. Two hundred vessels, grills on decks. Gloriously absurd.

5. MIDNIGHT YELL, TEXAS A&M. Ninety thousand people fill the stadium at midnight the night before the game to practice cheering. Not the game. The cheering. Cheer Practice you say? It's because the Aggies aren't real bright, but they are very nice. Feel free to @grok Aggie jokes.

6. AUBURN. Toomer's Corner, where the town throws toilet paper into the oak trees after a win, and a live eagle flies laps around the stadium before kickoff.

7. CLEMSON. The team touches a rock and runs down a hill into the stadium. Eighty thousand people lose their minds.

8. THE BOULEVARD, SMU. Dallas. Catered tents under the trees, genuinely elegant. Easy add if you are already there for Red River. Let me know I have a friend that can hook you up.

9. GEORGIA VERSUS FLORIDA, OCTOBER 31. Your warning. It is in ATLANTA this year, not Jacksonville, because the stadium is being renovated. The Cocktail Party without the RV city on the river is a different animal. Adjust expectations.

10. NOTRE DAME. The one exception to my stick-to-the-South rule, and worth breaking it for.

NOW THE THING NOBODY TELLS VISITORS.

Everyone talks about Friday Night Lights in Texas, and everyone pictures a dusty little town with a rusting water tower.

Allen reinvented the whole thing, and nobody does it better. Not the small towns. Not anybody.

Eighteen thousand seats at a single high school. A sixty million dollar stadium. A marching band of eight hundred, the largest in the country, covering the entire field at halftime. Record crowd 21,766. For teenagers. On a Friday.

Here is the insider move. Get there early and find the Balding Eagles booster club. Tell them you flew in from Europe to see this. They will feed you, they will talk your ear off, and there is a decent chance somebody walks you through the stadium. Americans cannot help themselves when a foreigner takes their town seriously.

And in Texas you can stack the whole weekend. High school Friday night, college Saturday, pro Sunday. Nowhere else on earth offers that, and the Friday night game will teach you more about this country than the other two combined.

BASEBALL, AND IT HITS DIFFERENTLY.

The honest problem is you cannot plan playoff baseball, because nobody knows who qualifies until the final week of September.

So plan geography instead of teams. Your route already passes the right cities. Atlanta has the Braves and you are there October 31. Texas has the Rangers and Astros and you are there October 10, right in division series week. Tampa Bay is in play if Florida is on the map.

Buy nothing until late September. When the brackets set, resale is how visitors get in.

If it does not fall your way, go the last week of September anyway. Teams fighting for a spot play like it is already October.

One conflict to check. The Breeders' Cup usually lands that same last weekend of October as Georgia-Florida.

Come hungry. Say yes when a stranger offers you food. That is the whole etiquette. Avoid the Taco Bell. Taco Bueno is the better option or find a real Tex-Mex place if you are in Texas. Avoid Tex Mex anywhere else.🦋

Since so many have asked recently; here’s a little about my background…I’m proud to say I am a direct descendant of both Kit Carson and William Ashley. Being a trail blazer has always been part of the family legacy. Which should tell you a bit about our family genome and personality type. We are not followers, we are leaders. 

Now for your enlightenment: 

Here is a list of 10 of the most significant American explorers and mountain men who played key roles in exploring, mapping, guiding, and opening the American frontier (primarily the trans-Appalachian and far western regions in the late 18th and 19th centuries). Their efforts facilitated fur trade, trail development, scientific/geographic knowledge, and eventual settlement by emigrants. Rankings of “top” figures are inherently subjective and draw from historical accounts of their impact. https://t.co/t60jJkLjr2 
1.  Daniel Boone (1734–1820) Frontiersman, long hunter, and pioneer who blazed the Wilderness Road through the Cumberland Gap in 1775. This route opened Kentucky and the trans-Appalachian West to large-scale American settlement, and he helped establish early communities such as Boonesborough. https://t.co/RXCkU470KY 
2.  Meriwether Lewis (1774–1809) Leader (with William Clark) of the Corps of Discovery (1804–1806). Commissioned by President Jefferson after the Louisiana Purchase, the expedition mapped a route to the Pacific, documented geography, flora, fauna, and Native peoples, and strengthened U.S. claims to the Northwest. https://t.co/t60jJkLjr2 
3.  William Clark (1770–1838) Co-leader of the Lewis and Clark Expedition. He served as primary mapmaker, diplomat with tribes, and military officer; his detailed journals and charts provided foundational knowledge of the Missouri River system and overland route to the Pacific that later informed fur traders and settlers. https://t.co/RXCkU470KY 
4.  Zebulon Pike (1779–1813) U.S. Army officer who led expeditions (1805–1807) exploring the upper Mississippi and the southwestern Louisiana Purchase (including the Great Plains, Arkansas River headwaters, and the peak later named for him). His reports offered early American descriptions of the region and routes that influenced later trade and expansion into the Southwest. https://t.co/t60jJkLjr2 
5.  John Colter (c. 1774–1813) Member of the Lewis and Clark Expedition who stayed in the West as one of the earliest mountain men and free trappers. He explored the Yellowstone region (reporting its geothermal features, later called “Colter’s Hell”), the Tetons, and surrounding areas, helping initiate the Rocky Mountain fur trade era. https://t.co/t60jJkLjr2 
6.  Jedediah Smith (1799–1831) Trapper, explorer, and fur company partner who rediscovered and popularized South Pass (a critical low crossing of the Rockies used by the Oregon Trail). He was among the first Americans to cross the Great Basin, reach California overland via the Mojave, travel the Pacific coast northward, and extensively map much of the intermountain West. https://t.co/t60jJkLjr2 
7.  Jim Bridger (1804–1881) Long-career mountain man, trapper, and guide who was among the first non-Natives to see the Great Salt Lake and Yellowstone features. He established Fort Bridger (a key Oregon Trail supply point), located Bridger’s Pass and other routes, and later guided army expeditions, railroad surveys, and emigrant parties with unmatched knowledge of the northern Rockies. https://t.co/zboMawvgiJ 
8.  Kit Carson (1809–1868) Trapper, scout, guide, Indian agent, and soldier. He guided John C. Frémont’s mapping expeditions through the Rockies, Great Basin, California, and Oregon; served as a wagon-train and military guide; and became a widely known figure whose knowledge and reports aided western expansion and settlement. https://t.co/t60jJkLjr2
